events.text: Late autumn, and the first snow is coming down as fine as rice flour. You are alone on the pass road at dusk, which is the one thing everybody in the village tells you never to be: the woodcutters cross this pass ten at a time with a gong, and they put the strongest at the back, because a tiger always takes the last in the line. You stayed too long at the market in the next valley. On a rock above the road, where there was no shape on the way over this morning, there is a shape now. It is striped. It is as long as an ox cart. It is looking at your bundle.

choices.text: Throw it the rice cakes from your bundle

effects.log: You unwrap the rice cakes you were carrying home and throw one onto the snow below the rock, and then, because your hands will not stop, all of them. The words from the old story come out of your mouth by themselves: here is a rice cake, so do not eat me. The striped thing comes down and eats every one with enormous seriousness. Then it looks at you for a long moment and goes back up the slope. All the way to the village lights it walks along the ridge above you, keeping pace, at a polite distance.

choices.text: Bow to the ground and call it your lost eldest

effects.log: You throw yourself face down in the snow and wail: "Eldest! Our eldest! Our mother says you were born in a tiger year and went into the mountains and never came home, and she weeps for you every night!" It is the stupidest lie you have ever told. The tiger stops halfway down the rock. Its ears go flat, then forward. It makes a small sound, almost a question. Then it turns and goes up into the trees, slowly, looking back twice. You run all the way home. In the morning there is a dead roe deer lying across your gate.

choices.text: Stand perfectly still and keep your head

ok.log: You do what the old people say: you do not run, you do not shout, you do not turn your back. You breathe. The tiger watches you breathe. The snow settles on both of you. After a time you could not count, it stands, stretches like a cat in front of a fire, and walks off along the ridge, and as it goes you see that the very tip of its tail is as white as the snow. Nobody in the village believes you about the tail.

fail.log: You stand still for as long as you can, which is not as long as you hoped. When your knees go and you sit down hard in the snow, the tiger tilts its head, puzzled, and leaves. As it goes you see a flash of white at the tip of its tail. (-6 health)

events.text: The county has posted a reward on the magistrate's gate: a man-eater on the western pass, eleven dead since spring, the bounty paid by the length of the pelt and doubled for whoever strikes first. {npc}, captain of the tiger-catching soldiers, takes you on for the season: a spear, a padded coat, a crane-head pouch of lead balls and a place in a line of twenty walking up the snow. On the third day the tracks bring you to a tiger with a white tip to its tail, and it is not the man-eater: it is following the man-eater's tracks too. And ahead of all of you on the path a figure in a torn white jacket is walking without leaving footprints, calling a child's name.

choices.text: Go for the white-tailed tiger: it is bigger, and the bounty is by size

ok.log: You strike first, which is what pays. The spear goes into the white-tailed tiger's shoulder and it turns on you, and for one moment you are looking straight down its throat. Then it is gone into the bamboo, bleeding, and you are alive, which you understand only later was its choice and not yours. {npc} pays you sixty taels for first blood. That night the man-eater takes its twelfth.

fail.log: Your spear goes past its ear. It knocks you down with one paw, the way you would knock a cup off a table, puts its face very close to yours, and does not bite. Then it is gone after the man-eater. {npc} hauls you out of the snow and says nothing at all, which from {npc} is a great deal. (-15 health)

choices.text: Hunt the real man-eater beside it

ok.log: You leave the line and go up the slope after the white tail, and it lets you. At the head of the ravine the man-eater is waiting, bigger and greyer and mangy, with the walking ghost standing beside it like a servant. It comes for you. The white-tailed tiger comes for it. Between the two of you it does not last long. Afterwards the white tiger looks at you across the body, steaming, and goes; and the ghost in the torn jacket stops calling, sits down in the snow, and is not there any more. {npc} measures the man-eater and pays the whole bounty to you.

fail.log: The man-eater comes out of the rocks before you are ready and you are down, its weight on you, its breath like a charnel pit. Then the weight is gone. When you can see again, the white-tailed tiger is standing over the dead man-eater and looking at you as if you were a disappointing cub. It leaves you the body, and the bounty. (-18 health)

choices.text: Lay down your spear before the mountain god's painting in the pass shrine

effects.log: At the top of the pass there is a little shrine, three stone slabs and a roof, with a plank painting inside: an old man with a white beard under a pine, and a striped tiger lying at the old knees. You lay your spear across the threshold and kneel. {npc} calls you a coward in front of the whole line. That night, asleep in the shrine, you dream of the old man, who says only: "Thank you. It has enough to carry." In the morning the man-eater is found dead at the foot of a cliff, and round it in the snow are the prints of one tiger, with a long brush-mark where a tail lay.

events.text: Autumn equinox, midnight. The seven stars of the western sky, Legs and Bond, Stomach and Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak and the Three Stars, come down out of heaven one after another and are a white tiger, its stripes made of night. It lies down along the west wall of your courtyard with its tail out past the gate, and every leaf on your trees falls at once. "Human," it says, "you are strong enough to be heard in heaven. Sit beside me as the human assessor. One case." The case stands in the frost before you: a ghost in a torn jacket, eaten by a tiger on a western pass a hundred years ago, which has called nine travellers to that same pass, one after another, in the voices of their mothers, so that one of them would take its place and set it free. Behind it, very large and very ashamed, sits the old tiger that ate it.

choices.text: Free the ghost: it was a traveller before it was a lure

effects.log: You say it plainly: before it was a lure it was somebody with a bundle on a road, and nobody ever laid it to rest. The white tiger of stars considers this for the time it takes a leaf to fall. Then it breathes out, and the ghost comes apart like frost in sun, and for one moment you see a young face, surprised, relieved. "Mercy," the tiger says. "Entered." In its chest the three straight stars of the Balance tip a hair's breadth toward you.

choices.text: Punish the ghost: nine died to buy its freedom

effects.log: "Nine for one is no bargain," you say. "It goes back under the pot and the spindle." The ghost screams without a sound. The tiger of stars nods slowly, and out of the sky comes an iron steamer pot, upside down, over the ghost, and an iron spindle through the hole in it, and inside the ghost begins to go round, and round, like thread on a wheel. "Severity," the tiger says. "Entered." You do not sleep well for a month, and you would say the same again.

choices.text: Put the tiger that ate it on trial instead

ok.log: "The ghost is the tiger's doing," you say. "Try the one with the teeth." The frost goes silent. The old tiger lowers its head to the ground. The tiger of stars looks at you for a long time, and then, for the first time, at the old tiger, and the case is heard again from the beginning with the right defendant. At the end the old tiger lays its ghost to rest with its own paws, under a cairn. "That," says the tiger of stars, "is the first time in a thousand years an assessor has corrected the court." It sounds delighted.

fail.log: You try to turn the case on the old tiger and lose the thread halfway through your own argument. The court growls; your ears ring. In the end the tiger of stars hears both of them, the ghost and the tiger, and divides the sentence between them, the way a grown person finishes a child's sum. (-10 health)

events.text: A year after the Autumn Court, a magpie lands on your gatepost at dawn and will not leave: white belly, black head, an eye full of impertinence. In its beak is a single white hair as long as your arm. Behind it, on the west side of your courtyard, the persimmon tree has dropped every leaf in one night.

choices.text: Take the hair from its beak

effects.log: It is warm, and it hums faintly, like a plucked string. You sew it into your collar. All that winter you know, without knowing how, which of the people who come to your gate are lying.

choices.text: Ask the magpie what the court decided in the end

effects.log: The magpie says nothing, being a magpie. But it hops westward along your wall three times, stops, and tips its head toward the western sky, where the three straight stars of the Balance hang very level tonight. You take that as an answer, and you think it was a good one.

choices.text: Shoo it off: you have done your part

effects.log: It goes, cackling. Magpies bring news, and you have refused it. For the rest of the year you hear everything last, which is less restful than it sounds.

events.text: {npc}, a clerk of the Western Palace in robes the colour of frost, finds you in the Upper Realm with a ledger tied shut with white cord. "Your verdict as assessor has been filed," {npc} says, "under the Three Stars, with the capital cases. The White Tiger asks whether you would sit again. The courts of heaven are short of humans. Humans remember what it is like to be judged."

choices.text: Sit again, for one more autumn

effects.log: One more autumn on a bench of white stone beside a tiger made of night. Cases come and go like leaves. You find that the hard thing is not deciding but keeping your hand level while you decide. At the end of it the tiger touches its nose to your forehead, cold as frost, and the clerk writes your name in the ledger in white ink.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that once was enough

effects.log: {npc} writes it down without surprise. "Most say that," {npc} says. "The good ones." Somewhere in the Western Palace a great white shape yawns, and every leaf in the Upper Realm turns gold at once.

events.text: Winter night. The baby of the house will not stop crying, and the grown-ups have gone to a funeral in the next village, so it is you who walks the baby up and down the warm floor. Outside, the snow creaks. Something is breathing at the paper window, slow and big, like a bellows. You remember what the old people say to crying children: hush, or the tiger will come. You say it. The baby cries louder. The breathing at the window stops, as if it were listening.

choices.text: Give the baby a dried persimmon from the string in the rafters

effects.log: "Here," you say, loudly, "here is a dried persimmon," and the baby, astonished, stops crying at once and sucks it. Outside there is a long silence. Then the snow creaks very fast, going away, as if something enormous had decided that whatever a dried persimmon was, it was worse than a tiger. In the morning there are paw prints as big as rice bowls under the window, and then a long panicked line of them going up the hill.

choices.text: Wet a finger, poke a hole in the window paper, and look

effects.log: You push your finger through the paper the way children do and put your eye to the hole. An eye looks back. It is amber, as big as your fist, and very close. It blinks once, slowly, the way a cat blinks at something it has decided not to eat. Then the window is only night and snow, and a flick of a white tail-tip going round the corner of the house.

choices.text: Sing the baby the lullaby, louder

effects.log: You sing the only song you know all the way through, twice, very badly. The baby falls asleep out of sheer exhaustion. Outside, the breathing settles into something slower, like a big animal lying down in the snow under the eaves to listen. When the grown-ups come home at dawn there is a hollow in the snow by the wall in the shape of a sleeping tiger, still warm.

events.text: Since the night on the pass you have taken to leaving a rice cake on the flat rock above the road whenever you cross, wrapped in an oak leaf. It is always gone the next time. This morning, on your own doorstep, there is a pheasant with its neck neatly broken and not one feather out of place.

choices.text: Cook it, and share it round the lane

effects.log: It is the best meal the lane has had all winter. The old woman next door, gnawing a wing, asks where it came from. You say "the pass". She stops chewing, looks at you, and then goes on, very thoughtfully.

choices.text: Leave two rice cakes on the rock next time

effects.log: Two rice cakes on the rock. The next week a hare on the doorstep, and the week after, a heap of chestnuts in a neat pile. The lane begins to say your house has a guardian. The lane is right.

choices.text: Stop leaving cakes: you have been lucky enough

effects.log: You stop. Nothing more comes to the door. But once, crossing the pass alone at dusk, you look up and see the striped shape on the rock, watching you go by with what you would swear is hurt feelings.

events.text: A widow from the far valley is crossing the pass at dusk with a basket of rice cakes on her head, for two children waiting at home. You see her from the village end of the road, too late to call her back. On the rock above the road something striped is getting up. And beside it is a second shape, bigger and greyer and crueller in the shoulders.

choices.text: Run up the road after her

ok.log: You catch her at the foot of the rock, breathless, and walk beside her with your arm through hers, talking loudly about nothing. The grey one slides down the slope toward you. The white-tipped one gets in its way with a sound like a millstone turning, and the grey one stops, and thinks, and goes. The widow gives you every rice cake in her basket and weeps. You give one back, for the rock.

fail.log: You fall on the ice and lose a sandal and come up the road limping. By the time you reach the rock the widow is sitting in the snow with her basket spilled, unhurt, and two tigers are walking away from her in two directions, one of them looking back at the other with its ears flat. (-10 health)

choices.text: Beat a pot and shout, the way the porters do

effects.log: You bang a cooking pot with a ladle and bellow until the whole village comes out with torches and gongs. The widow comes down the pass at a run, basket and all. Up on the rock the white-tipped shape sits down again and, you would swear, looks pleased with you.

events.text: Years later you hear the old story told at a winter fire, by a grandmother to a ring of children: the mother on the pass, the tiger that said give me a rice cake and I won't eat you, the brother and sister who climbed to the sky on a rope. But this grandmother tells it differently. In her version there were two tigers on the pass, and one of them stood in the other's way.

choices.text: Tell the children that part is true

effects.log: The children look at you with enormous suspicion. The grandmother looks at you with something else. When they are asleep she pours you a cup of barley tea and says only, "I knew somebody saw it."

choices.text: Ask her where she heard it

effects.log: "From the widow of the far valley," she says. "My mother. She said a stranger ran up the road with only one sandal on." She looks down at your feet, and laughs until she cries.

events.text: Since the night you called the tiger on the pass your lost eldest, game has been arriving at the gate. A roe deer laid neatly across the threshold. A pheasant. Last night a whole wild boar, which took two neighbours to drag in. The old woman of your house, who has heard the whole story and does not believe a word of it, stands over the boar with her hands on her hips. "Well," she says. "If it is your eldest, it is a better child than you."

choices.text: Keep the lie going: set out a bowl of rice for the eldest

effects.log: Every night you set a bowl of white rice and a cup of water on the flat stone by the gate, as you would for a child coming home late. Every morning the bowl is licked clean and something is lying across the threshold. The village begins to say your family is blessed.

choices.text: Confess the lie to the old woman

effects.log: She listens, cuffs you round the head, and then sets out a bowl of rice by the gate herself. "A tiger that keeps a promise you never made," she says, "deserves its supper." She does it every night after that, until she is too old to bend.

choices.text: Sell the boar at the market

effects.log: Eight taels for the boar. The next morning there is nothing at the gate, and the morning after, nothing, and on the third morning a single long white hair caught on the thorns of the hedge, like a word left unsaid.

events.text: The village has decided your household is the luckiest under the mountain: game at the gate, no thief in ten years, and the old woman of the house hale at an age when her friends are all in the hill graves. At dusk, on the ridge above the house, a great striped shape sits looking down at your gate, as it does every evening, with something in the set of its head that might be pride.

choices.text: Bow to the ridge each evening, as to an elder

effects.log: You start bowing to the ridge at dusk, the way a younger sibling bows to the eldest at the New Year. The neighbours think you have gone strange. The first time you do it, the shape on the ridge stands up, and stays standing until you have finished.

choices.text: Climb up and sit beside it, once

ok.log: You climb to the ridge in the dusk and sit down a body-length away. It does not move. The two of you look down at the little roof with its thread of smoke, as two siblings might, and you begin to believe your own lie, and that frightens you less than you thought it would.

fail.log: Halfway up the slope it gets up and walks away: not angrily, but the way an elder leaves a room when a younger one gets too familiar. You slip on the way down. (-8 health)

events.text: The old woman of your house has died, very old. On the night of the burial the mourners at the grave hear a sound from the mountain that they will talk about for the rest of their lives: a long low cry, over and over, not a roar, the way a person keens. In the morning a dead deer is lying on the fresh mound like an offering, and all round the grave, in the frost, are the prints of one great tiger walking in circles.

choices.text: Wear the hemp three years, and keep setting out the bowl

effects.log: Three years in mourning hemp. Every night a bowl at the gate, and every morning it is empty. On the last night of the mourning there is nothing at the gate at all, and you understand that the mourning is over, for both of you.

choices.text: Go up the mountain and grieve with it

effects.log: You find it lying on a ledge above the grave, not eating. You sit with it and talk about her: how she cuffed you, the bowl of rice. After a long time it gets up and goes, and that evening, you learn later, it ate for the first time in a week.

events.text: Since the evening on the pass you dream, now and then, of standing still in the snow while something breathes. Tonight in the dream it speaks, in a voice like gravel turning over in a stream: "You did not run. Everyone runs. When they run, I am a tiger. When they stand still, I have to decide what I am."

choices.text: Ask it what it decided

effects.log: "Not yet," it says. "I am young. Four hundred years, perhaps, before I know." You wake with snow-cold feet in a warm room, and with the odd conviction that you have been handed a very long promissory note.

choices.text: Tell it to decide to be kind

effects.log: "Kind," it repeats, as if tasting a strange food. "Kind to whom? The deer?" A long silence. "I will think about it." You wake, and for a whole winter you find you cannot kill so much as a chicken for the pot.

events.text: A long time after the dream, crossing a western pass, you see it again: on a rock above the road, enormous now, its tail white not only at the tip but halfway up. It looks at you. You stand still, out of old habit. So does it. Then it inclines its head a fraction, the way one old acquaintance greets another across a market.

choices.text: Bow back

effects.log: You bow, deeply. When you straighten up the rock is empty, and you walk the rest of the pass with the feeling of being escorted by somebody too polite to be seen.

choices.text: Ask it, aloud, what it decided

effects.log: "Mostly kind," it says from the rock, in a human voice that has plainly had a great deal of practice. "Not always. The pass is safer than it was." Then, drily: "You are still very good at standing."

events.text: Every winter since the night at the window a string of dried persimmons hangs from your eaves, and every winter, on the coldest night, one is gone in the morning: the string bitten through, neatly, and the snow under the window pressed flat in the shape of something large that sat there a long while.

choices.text: Hang a second string, lower down

effects.log: Both strings are bitten in the morning, one persimmon from each, as if out of fairness. On the doorstep is a pheasant. The grown-ups argue about it for a week. You keep very quiet.

choices.text: Stay up to watch

ok.log: Near the third watch it comes, a striped tiger as long as an ox cart, and sits under the eaves and eats one persimmon very slowly with its eyes shut, like someone facing a great fear and finding it sweet. Its tail-tip is white. It sees your eye at the finger-hole, and leaves the stone on the windowsill.

fail.log: You fall asleep sitting up against the wall. In the morning one persimmon is gone, and on the windowsill, set down carefully, is its stone.

events.text: Grown, you hear a storyteller at the market tell the old tale of the tiger and the dried persimmon: the tiger at the window, the baby, the persimmon it took for a monster, the cow thief in the dark who jumped on its back, and the tiger running for its life with a thief clinging on. The crowd roars. You find you are not laughing. You are remembering an eye at a finger-hole.

choices.text: Tell the storyteller that the tiger came back for the persimmons

effects.log: The storyteller adds it at once. Within a year it is the ending everyone knows: the tiger learned what a dried persimmon was, liked it, and came back every winter. Children leave them on their windowsills for it. You are absurdly proud.

choices.text: Hang a string of persimmons from your own eaves this winter

effects.log: One is gone on the coldest night, the string bitten through, and the snow under the window is pressed into a shape you know. You stand in the doorway in the morning grinning like a child.

events.text: The man-eater you did not hunt has taken four more since the season you put your spear into the white-tailed tiger instead. The magistrate has raised the reward. And every night now you dream of a figure in a torn white jacket walking ahead of you up a snowy path, calling a child's name, and every night the name sounds a little more like yours.

choices.text: Go back up the pass alone and finish the right tiger

ok.log: Three nights on the pass. On the third the man-eater comes for you out of the rocks with its ghost walking in front, and you are ready, and it is over. The ghost stops in the snow, turns, and bows to you. On the ridge a white-tailed tiger with a healed scar on its shoulder watches the whole thing and does not come down.

fail.log: It nearly has you. What saves you is a second tiger coming down out of the trees, one with a white tail and a long scar on its shoulder where your spear went in. It kills the man-eater and leaves without looking at you, which is worse than anything it could have done. (-20 health)

choices.text: Give sixty taels to the families of the dead (60 taels)

effects.log: Sixty taels, shared among the households of the dead. It brings nobody back. But that night, in the dream, the figure in the torn jacket stops calling and walks on alone.

choices.text: Tell yourself a bounty is a bounty

effects.log: The dreams do not stop. You learn to sleep through them, which you will come to regret.

events.text: {npc}, the captain who paid you for first blood on the white-tailed tiger, has a new commission and has come to find you. The court wants a white tiger pelt for the dais of the throne hall, and has heard of a tiger with a white tail on the western pass. "Size and first strike," {npc} says. "Same terms. You know the beast. Four hundred men this time."

choices.text: Refuse, and warn the pass

effects.log: You refuse. Then you walk to the western pass alone and sit on the road at dusk three nights running, until on the third something huge sits down on the rock above you. You tell it everything: four hundred men, the dais, the court. It listens. In spring the great hunt finds nothing on the western pass but a magpie that laughs at it.

choices.text: Join, and lead them the wrong way

ok.log: Forty days in the wrong mountains. {npc} begins to suspect around the thirtieth and says nothing, which tells you more about {npc} than anything else ever has.

fail.log: {npc} sees through you on the second day and sends you home under guard. But you have cost them a week, and a week is a long time on a mountain. (-10 health)

choices.text: Join for the silver

effects.log: Eighty taels in advance. The white tail is never found that season. But you have chosen, and somewhere on the western pass something has heard you choose.

events.text: {npc} has made you an officer of the tiger-catchers. The work is mostly arithmetic: a pelt is paid by the foot, first blood is paid double, and the county pays nothing at all for a tiger that only eats deer. "There is a white-tailed one on the western pass," {npc} says over the fire. "Big. It would pay the whole company for a year. It has never touched a person, as far as anyone knows." Everyone round the fire looks at you.

choices.text: Argue to strike it off the list

ok.log: You argue all night: a tiger that kills man-eaters is the cheapest soldier the county has. In the morning {npc} crosses the white tail off the ledger with one stroke, and writes beside it, in small letters: ally.

fail.log: {npc} hears you out and does not cross it off. But {npc} sends nobody after it, that season or the next, and every time the company passes the western pass you see {npc} look up at the ridge, and nod.

choices.text: Say nothing: the company needs the silver

effects.log: Thirty taels each, if it is ever caught. It is never caught. The company stops talking about it after a year, the way people stop talking about a debt they suspect they owe.

events.text: A season of man-eaters, three of them on three passes, and your company is spread thin. On the third pass you are alone with two young soldiers when a ghost comes down the path ahead of its tiger, calling one of them by name in the voice of the one who raised him, and the boy starts walking toward it.

choices.text: Grab him and hold on

ok.log: You get both arms round him and he fights you like a drowning man, weeping, all the way down the path. The voice follows you for a mile, and then it gives up. He will not speak of it for a year. Then one night by the fire he thanks you, and cannot finish.

fail.log: He breaks free and you go after him and the tiger comes out of the rocks at both of you. You get him back down the path with a gash across your back. (-15 health)

choices.text: Strike the gong, the way the old porters did

effects.log: You beat the gong until it cracks. The voice falters. From the ridge comes an answer, a roar like a landslide, and the ghost and the tiger behind it both stop. Then the man-eater goes, and its ghost with it. You know whose roar that was. You leave it out of the report.

events.text: You keep going back to the shrine at the top of the pass. Nobody else tends it. The roof slabs have slipped, and the plank painting of the old man and the tiger has been rained on so long that the tiger is only a stripe or two and an eye. Tonight, sweeping out the leaves, you find a bowl of clean water on the little altar that you did not bring.

choices.text: Mend the roof and repaint the tiger

ok.log: A season of slabs and plaster, then a month with a borrowed brush. You paint the tiger as you saw it on the bounty hunt: big, white-tipped, embarrassed. When you step back, the old man in the painting is smiling at the tiger, which you did not paint.

fail.log: The roof is fine. The tiger you paint looks like a cat that has swallowed a wasp. In the morning there is one long white hair laid across the threshold, the way a critic leaves a note.

choices.text: Leave a cup of rice wine and a rice cake, and sit the night

effects.log: You sit up with the candles. Near dawn the cup is empty and the rice cake gone, and nothing came in at the door that you saw. Two candles, a bowl of water, and a keeper: the shrine seems to feel that is the right number of things.

events.text: The villages under the pass call you the shrine keeper now. Travellers who must cross after dark come to you first, and you walk them to the top and light the candle, and they go over in a group, singing. Tonight a child comes alone, with a jar of medicine for a dying parent on the far side, who cannot wait for morning.

choices.text: Carry the child over yourself

effects.log: Halfway over, in the dark, you notice that something has fallen into step with you on the ridge above, very large and very quiet, keeping pace like an escort. You deliver the child and the medicine before dawn. On the way back, alone, the escort walks beside you openly, its white tail swinging, all the way to the shrine.

choices.text: Light the candle and ask the old man of the mountain to carry the child

effects.log: You light the candle, say the words, and set the child on the path. The child goes into the dark alone, which is the hardest thing you have ever allowed. At dawn the child is back, beaming: "A big cat carried me. It was warm. It smelled like pine." The medicine was delivered. You do not explain.

events.text: On a western pass you come on a cairn with a steamer pot turned upside down on top of it and an iron spindle driven through its hole, and you know it the way you would know your own handwriting: it is your sentence from the Autumn Court. Inside the pot, faintly, something is going round and round, like thread on a spinning wheel. It has been going round since that night.

choices.text: Pull out the spindle

effects.log: The iron comes out cold. Something rises from the pot like breath on a winter morning, hesitates, and goes west. Severity, you think, is also a thing you can take back, if you are willing to be the one who looks foolish.

choices.text: Leave it: the sentence was just

effects.log: You stand by the cairn until dusk. On the far ridge a white tail moves once, slowly, and is still. You take it to mean that the court agrees, and also that it is sorry. Both can be true.

events.text: A young traveller with a bundle on {his} back stops at your gate to ask the way over the western pass. {npc} has never crossed it, {he} says, but has dreamed of it all {his} life: snow, a rock above the road, and somebody kind telling a court of stars that {he} was a traveller before {he} was anything else.

choices.text: Walk {npc} over the pass yourself

effects.log: You cross together at noon, the safest hour. At the top {npc} stops on one exact spot, shivers, and laughs. "Here," {he} says. "It was here." Then {he} goes on down the other side, free, and you watch until {he} is out of sight.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to cross in a group, with a gong

effects.log: {npc} thanks you, puzzled at how serious you are. You hear later that {he} crossed with twelve woodcutters and a gong, and that a white-tailed tiger sat on a rock above the road and watched them pass and did not move, as if it were counting.

events.text: The old tiger whose case you turned at the Autumn Court comes to your gate on a night of first frost. It is grey to the muzzle, and it lies down outside your wall like a dog that has walked a long way. In its mouth is a broken iron spindle.

choices.text: Take the spindle from it

effects.log: It lets you. "Laid to rest," it says, in a voice like a door that has not been opened in a century. "All of mine. One by one. It took eighty years." It sleeps by your wall until dawn and goes, lighter by eighty years.

choices.text: Bring it water and meat

effects.log: It drinks, and eats a little, politely, like an old guest. In the morning the spindle is lying on your step, and the frost on the courtyard has melted in the shape of a great sleeping cat.

events.text: Winter night by the brazier. The old woman who keeps the brazier tells the one about the brother and sister: the mother crossing the hills with a basket of rice cakes, the tiger at every pass saying give me a rice cake and I won't eat you, until there were no rice cakes and no mother; the tiger in her clothes at the door, the hairy hand through the paper; the children up the tree, and the rope from heaven. "And heaven sent the tiger a rope too," she says, "a rotten one. It fell on the sorghum field, and that is why sorghum stalks are red."

choices.text: Ask why heaven sent the tiger a rope at all

effects.log: "Because it asked," she says. "Heaven gives what is asked for. It does not always give it whole." She pokes the coals. "Be careful what you ask for while you are wearing somebody else's clothes."

choices.text: Say you would have given the tiger every rice cake at the first pass

effects.log: "Then it would have eaten you at the second," she says, "and you would be a very generous ghost." But she looks pleased, and gives you the last chestnut.

choices.text: Go out to the shed and look at the sorghum stalks

effects.log: By lamplight the cut sorghum in the shed is red at the foot of every stalk, as if stained. You go back to bed and lie awake a long time thinking about falling.

events.text: Harvesting sorghum on the hill field in autumn, you come to a patch in the middle where every stalk is red from root to tassel, redder than any in the valley, and the ground under it is pressed down in a long shape, as if something heavy had once fallen there from a very great height.

choices.text: Cut it with the rest

effects.log: It goes into the stack with the rest. That winter the spirit distilled from the red sorghum is the strongest in the county, and the old men who drink it go quiet and say it tastes of something they cannot name. Regret, you think, and keep it to yourself.

choices.text: Leave the red patch standing

effects.log: You harvest round it. All winter the red patch stands alone in the snow, and on the coldest night something sits beside it, and in the morning there are paw prints all round it and none leading in or out.

events.text: Burning charcoal on the mountain for the winter trade, you have to sit up with the kiln three nights running so the fire neither dies nor breaks through the earth. On the second night a tiger walks out of the dark and lies down on the far side of the kiln, the way a dog lies down by a hearth, and shuts its eyes against the heat.

choices.text: Keep feeding the kiln, and talk to it

effects.log: You talk all night because the silence is worse: the price of charcoal, the magistrate's new tax, somebody in the next village you are sweet on. It listens with its eyes shut. At dawn it gets up, stretches, and goes. You have never had a better audience.

choices.text: Climb onto the kiln roof, out of reach

ok.log: You spend the night on the hot earth roof, steaming, while the tiger dozes below. In the morning it yawns up at you, showing every tooth, which you choose to take as a joke.

fail.log: The roof gives under you and you are in the smoke, coughing and singed. When you crawl out the tiger is sitting a little way off, watching with what looks like real concern. (-8 health)

choices.text: Throw it the dried fish from your pack

effects.log: It eats the fish in two bites and looks at your pack with frank interest. You give it the other one. After that it comes every winter on the second night of the burn, and you bring three fish.

events.text: The third winter at the kiln. Tonight it is not your tiger that comes out of the dark. This one is bigger and greyer, with a torn ear and a smell of carrion, and it is not lying down.

choices.text: Swing a burning brand at it

ok.log: You come at it with a pine brand in each hand, roaring. It backs off, snarling, and circles the kiln twice, and then a second shape comes out of the trees behind it, stiff-legged, with a white tip to its tail, and the grey one decides the night is not worth it.

fail.log: It knocks the brand out of your hand and you go down in the snow. Then there are two tigers over you, and a sound like a millstone, and the grey one is gone, and your own tiger is licking a torn shoulder on the far side of the kiln. (-18 health)

choices.text: Shout the name you gave your tiger

effects.log: You shout it, feeling absurd. The grey tiger stops. From the trees behind it comes a sound like a millstone turning, and your own tiger walks into the firelight, stiff-legged. The two of them look at each other over the kiln for a long time. The grey one goes. Your tiger lies down in its usual place as if nothing had happened, and you feed the kiln with shaking hands until dawn.

events.text: On the road to the county school with your books on your back, you come round a bend and there is a tiger in the path. It is not crouching. It is sitting with its mouth wide open and its eyes streaming, making a terrible small sound, and when it sees you it does not spring: it opens its mouth wider and looks at you, the way a child holds up a cut finger. Wedged crosswise in its throat is a long splinter of bone.

choices.text: Put your arm in and pull it out

ok.log: Your whole arm to the elbow, its breath hot on your shoulder, its teeth on either side of you like a fence. The bone comes out with a jerk. The tiger coughs, shakes its head, and looks at you for a long moment with an expression you will never forget. Then it bows. Tigers do not bow. This one does.

fail.log: The bone comes out, and so does a good deal of your sleeve and some of your skin on the way back past its teeth. It did not bite. It simply could not help being made of knives. It licks your arm once, rough as a file, and goes. (-10 health)

choices.text: Work it loose with your long hairpin

ok.log: With the hairpin you lever the bone sideways until it drops. The tiger takes the hairpin very carefully in its teeth, as if that were the important thing, and carries it off into the forest.

fail.log: The pin snaps. The tiger coughs the bone up by itself in the end, glares at you as if you had made things worse, and goes. Fair.

choices.text: Back away slowly, then run

effects.log: You run all the way to the school. For weeks afterwards you think about the sound it was making, and wish, a little, that you were braver.

events.text: You have failed the state examination. Again: the third time. You walk home over the mountain with your inkstone in your sleeve, wondering how to tell everyone, and at the top of the pass, sitting in the road as if waiting for a friend, is the tiger whose throat you cleared.

choices.text: Sit down beside it and tell it everything

effects.log: You tell it about the examination hall, the hard bench, the questions you knew and answered badly. It listens. When you have finished it gets up and walks three times round you, slowly, as if it were making a plan. Then it goes.

choices.text: Ask it, half joking, to make your fortune

effects.log: "Well," you say, "you owe me." It looks at you for a long time, very seriously, as if you had said the thing it had been waiting to hear. Then it goes. You have an uneasy feeling that a contract has just been signed.

events.text: Market day in the county town, and a tiger walks into the square at noon. People scatter, screaming. It touches none of them. It walks straight through the stalls to where you are standing, stops, and lies down at your feet with its throat to the sky. The whole town is watching. The county has a standing reward and a post for whoever kills a tiger inside the walls.

choices.text: Take its life, as it is asking you to

effects.log: It does not fight. Afterwards the magistrate gives you fifty taels and a post, the whole county calls you a hero, and you never once in your life tell the true story aloud. You keep the bone from its throat on a cord round your neck, and on autumn nights it is warm.

choices.text: Roar and wave your arms: be the hero who drove it off

ok.log: You roar at it like a madman. It looks at you, understands, and gets up and flees, magnificently, scattering a stall of cabbages, out of the gate and up the mountain. The town cannot stop talking about the student who shouted down a tiger. The county gives you a small post. Somewhere, a tiger is very pleased with its acting.

fail.log: Your shout cracks in the middle. The tiger waits patiently for you to try again. In the end it gets bored and leaves on its own, and the town decides it simply was not hungry. It was a kind thought, on both sides.

choices.text: Kneel beside it and refuse, in front of everyone

effects.log: You kneel in the dust of the square, put your hand on its head, and say no, loudly, so that it can hear. The town decides you are mad, or a sorcerer. After a while the tiger gets up and walks out the way it came, and nobody dares stop it. You never pass the examination. You never need to: the story follows you, and people come from three counties to be taught by the student the tiger loved.

events.text: New Year. You buy a magpie-and-tiger painting from the folk painter at the market to paste on the gate against evil for the year: a magpie chattering on a pine branch, and under it a tiger drawn so silly, cross-eyed and grinning with its tail in a curl, that the children shriek. The painter says the sillier the tiger, the better it works. "Evil cannot stand being laughed at by a magpie," he says. "Neither can a magistrate."

choices.text: Paste it on the gate

effects.log: It goes up crooked, which the painter says is lucky. All down the lane the same silly tiger grins from every gate, and the magpies on the real pines look down at them with satisfaction.

choices.text: Ask him why the tiger is a fool

effects.log: "Because the tiger is the yangban," he whispers, "and the magpie is us." He winks. "Also it is a tiger. Both. That is why it works." You paste it up and look at it for a long time.

events.text: In the night after New Year, something stands at your gate for a long time, looking at the painting. In the morning there are paw prints as big as rice bowls in the snow in front of it, and the painting has been licked, carefully, all over the tiger's silly face, until the paper is soft and the ink has run, and the tiger now looks, if anything, rather dignified.

choices.text: Buy a new painting with a handsomer tiger (2 taels)

effects.log: The painter is offended by the request and paints the handsomest tiger of his life, out of spite. The next night it is not licked. The night after, a pheasant is left beneath it, as a tip.

choices.text: Leave the licked one up all year

effects.log: The neighbours laugh at your soggy tiger all year. It is, you notice, the only gate in the lane that no fever comes through.

events.text: A tiger has taken two dogs and a calf this month, and the headman has put the young guards on tiger watch: one night each on the log platform at the top of the lane, with a pine torch, a brass gong, and orders to beat it the moment anything moves. Tonight is yours. At the third watch two lights come out of the black forest at the height of a person's chest and stop, side by side, looking at you.

choices.text: Beat the gong with all your strength

effects.log: The whole village pours out with torches and pots. The two lights go out. In the morning there are prints at the edge of the forest, the headman praises you, and you lie awake for a week remembering how calm the lights had been.

choices.text: Hold the torch high and stare back

ok.log: You stare. It stares. After a long time the lights blink, once, slowly, and go out, and the next month nothing is taken from the village at all. You never tell anybody that you did not beat the gong.

fail.log: Your hand shakes and the torch drops off the platform into the snow, and you are alone in the dark with the lights. They come no closer. When the next guard climbs up at dawn you are still sitting there with burned fingers, staring. (-6 health)

choices.text: Throw down the leg of mutton from your supper

effects.log: It lands in the snow at the edge of the trees. The lights look at it, and at you, and one of them goes out as if something had winked. In the morning the mutton is gone and so, for that month, are the killings.

events.text: You are escorting a string of salt porters over the pass at dusk because nobody else on the watch would go: twelve of them, a gong, and you at the very back, because everyone knows a tiger always takes the last one in the line. Something is walking beside you in the trees. You can hear it, a soft weight, keeping pace.

choices.text: Stay at the back: it is your job

ok.log: You walk the whole pass at the back with your spear reversed and your heart in your mouth. It keeps pace all the way and never comes out. On the far side the porters count themselves, twelve, and you count yourself, one. You have never been so glad to be a number.

fail.log: Halfway down it comes at you, low and fast. You get the spear up, just, and it veers off with a gash on its shoulder and is gone. The porters carry you the rest of the way. (-15 health)

choices.text: Put the loudest porter at the back and make everyone sing

effects.log: You put the fat salt porter at the back with the gong and set the whole line singing a vulgar song about a magistrate at the top of their lungs. Nothing on earth would attack that. Nothing does.

events.text: Years after the night on the platform, in a strange county, you sit up late at an inn window, and two lights come out of the forest and stop, side by side, at the height of a person's chest. You have looked at those lights before.

choices.text: Raise your cup to them

effects.log: The lights blink once, slowly. You drink. They go out. In the morning the innkeeper tells you, very puzzled, that the tiger which has troubled the village for a year has gone over the mountain in the night and left a dead boar at the inn gate.

choices.text: Go out to the edge of the forest

ok.log: It is sitting just inside the trees, much bigger than you remember, with a white tip to its tail now. It looks at you the way you would look at a child you once knew who has grown up: assessing, and, you think, approving. Then it goes.

fail.log: There is nothing there but cold and a branch across your face. When you get back to the window the lights are there again, and you could swear they are laughing. (-5 health)

events.text: {npc}, a boy from the village who wants very badly to be a hero, is digging a pit-trap across the deer path above the fields, with sharpened bamboo stakes in the bottom, for the tiger that has been taking calves. {npc} is proud of it. It is a good pit. It is also exactly where the woodcutters' children cut through on their way to the stream.

choices.text: Help {npc} move it off the children's path

effects.log: An afternoon of digging. {npc} sulks, then gets interested in the arithmetic of where a tiger would really walk, and the new pit is better. Nothing falls into it all autumn but leaves.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the story of the rabbit's judgement

effects.log: A traveller frees a tiger from a pit; the tiger means to eat the traveller; the pine and the ox, who have no love for people, say that is fair; the rabbit asks to see how it all began, and the tiger climbs back into the pit to show it. {npc} listens with the shovel forgotten. "So the pit was right?" "No," you say. "The rabbit was."

choices.text: Fill it in quietly after {npc} goes home

effects.log: You fill it in by moonlight. {npc} is heartbroken in the morning and blames a badger. You let the badger take it.

events.text: {npc} comes running down the hill as white as rice paper: something has fallen into a pit. Not the new one: an old one from years ago, overgrown, that nobody remembered. At the bottom, with a stake through one hind leg, is a striped tiger, and it is looking up at the two of you.

choices.text: Slide a log down and stand well back

ok.log: The tiger looks at the log, and at you, and climbs out on three legs. At the top it stops. You remember the story, and so, you think, does it. It does not eat you. It limps away into the trees, and {npc} sits down in the grass and cries from fright.

fail.log: It comes up the log faster than you expected and you are knocked flat. It stands over you for a long moment, breathing. Then it limps away into the trees. (-12 health)

choices.text: Send {npc} for the village and the spears

effects.log: The village comes with spears. It is not a fair fight and it is not a long one. {npc} is the hero of the lane for a year. You find you cannot look at the pelt where it hangs in the headman's house.

choices.text: Ask it, out loud, whether it means to eat you if you free it

effects.log: You feel foolish asking. It looks at you for so long that {npc} pulls at your sleeve. Then, very slowly, it lies down at the bottom of the pit with its chin on its paws: not a yes, not a no. You go and fetch the log.

events.text: Your elder sends you down to the county town with a purse: tiger bone, for the strengthening wine the elders drink at the winter solstice. Everybody knows market tiger bone is cow bone with a story. But {npc}, the old apothecary in the alley behind the salt market, unwraps a bone on a square of silk that is heavy as iron and faintly warm, and caught in a crack of it is a single long white hair.

choices.text: Buy it (15 taels)

effects.log: Fifteen taels, more than the elder gave you; you make up the rest from your own purse. {npc} wraps it twice and will not meet your eye.

choices.text: Ask {npc} where it came from

effects.log: "A pass in the west," {npc} says, low. "Hunters found an old tiger dead of age, white at the tail, and made an elixir of the bones for the court. I took one bone and no more." {npc} wraps it up again. "I think something walks that pass looking for its grandmother's bones."

choices.text: Buy cow bone and keep the difference

effects.log: The wine is as useless as everyone expected. The elders drink it anyway and feel wonderful, which teaches you something about medicine.

events.text: The night after the apothecary, something follows you back to the hall. You hear it on the roof tiles, a soft weight, and at the paper window, breathing, and once, just before dawn, a voice that is not quite a voice, very old, in the dark of your room: "That is my grandmother."

choices.text: Lay the bone on the windowsill and open the shutter

effects.log: In the morning the bone is gone and the sill is wet, as if licked. Your elder is furious about the purse. You find you do not mind at all.

choices.text: Brew the wine as your elder ordered

effects.log: The elixir is everything they say. That winter, every night, something sits outside the wall of the hall where you sleep, and does not come in, and does not go away.

choices.text: Bury it under a pine on the mountain and bow

effects.log: You dig with your hands under the oldest pine you can find and bow three times. On the way down a magpie follows you, chattering, from tree to tree, all the way to the gate, like a messenger with good news to deliver.

events.text: Benighted on a high pass with no inn for a day in either direction, you sleep against the wall of the little mountain god shrine at the top, with your sword across your knees and your back to the wind. You wake once in the night because the wind has stopped. Something warm and huge is lying curled round you on the windward side, breathing slowly, and you can feel its heart through your back like a drum in another room.
events.arc: The Shrine on the High Pass

choices.text: Lie still and go back to sleep

ok.log: You sleep, unbelievably, like a child. You wake at dawn on the far side of the pass, at the foot of the road, with your sword and your bundle laid neatly beside you and the shrine a long way above. You have no idea how you got there. There is a white hair on your cloak.

fail.log: You lie still and do not sleep a wink. At first light the warmth gets up and goes, and you see a striped back and a white tail-tip vanish into the mist, and you sit up very slowly with every hair on your body standing.

choices.text: Draw your sword, very slowly

ok.log: The sword is a hand out of its sheath when a heavy chin settles on your shoulder, the way a dog's does, and a breath like a furnace says, without words, no. You put the sword back. In the morning you are alone.

fail.log: One paw moves, lazily, and your sleeve and the skin under it open from elbow to wrist. Then it goes back to sleep. You sit awake till dawn bleeding into your cloak and feeling extremely rude. (-8 health)

events.text: You pass the shrine on the high pass again, years later. Somebody has mended its slabs and repainted the plank inside: the old man of the mountain under his pine, the tiger at his knee, and, curled asleep against the shrine wall at the very edge of the painting, very small, a traveller with a sword.
events.arc: The Shrine on the High Pass

choices.text: Leave an offering: a cup of wine and your best rice cake

effects.log: You set them on the altar beside the bowl of clean water and bow. Walking down the far side you find your legs are not tired, and do not get tired, all the way to the next town.

choices.text: Sleep there again, on purpose

effects.log: You lie down against the wall at dusk. Nothing comes. Toward midnight a pine cone drops on your head from a tree that is not there, and you laugh aloud in the dark, and sleep very well.

events.text: The tiger-catching corps is recruiting. {npc}, a sergeant with a claw scar from eye to jaw, lays out the terms on a table in the county yard: a spear, a padded coat, a matchlock so heavy that one soldier steadies it on a shoulder while another fires, a pouch made from the skin of a crane's head with its beak tied shut, and pay by the tiger: so much a foot of pelt, double to whoever strikes first. "Most of my recruits die of wanting to strike first," {npc} says. "Sign here."

choices.text: Sign, and ask how to live long

effects.log: "Be the second spear," {npc} says. "Never the first, never the last. The first gets the money. The last gets eaten. The second gets old."

choices.text: Sign, and mean to strike first every time

effects.log: {npc} looks at you the way a carpenter looks at green timber. "Good," {npc} says. "We always need a first spear." It is not, you realise later, a compliment.

choices.text: Decline: you will not kill by the foot

effects.log: {npc} shrugs and calls the next one forward. As you leave the yard a magpie on the gate laughs at somebody, and you are fairly sure it is not you.

events.text: Your first real hunt: a tiger that has taken a woman at a well. Forty beaters working up a ravine with gongs and drums, and you on the flank with a spear. The tiger breaks out of the brush not ten paces from you, flattened, fast, and it is not the size the sergeant promised. It is bigger.

choices.text: Strike first

ok.log: First blood, a hand-span into the shoulder. Then it is on you, and then it is not, because nine other spears have arrived. The pelt measures eleven feet. You are paid double. Your hands do not stop shaking for three days.

fail.deathCause: a man-eater in a ravine, striking first for the double pay
fail.log: You are first. That is all you are.

choices.text: Be the second spear

ok.log: Somebody else is first, and screams. You are second, and your spear goes in behind the shoulder where it counts. The first spear lives, just. You are paid the ordinary rate and sleep well.

fail.log: You are second, and late. A paw catches you across the thigh as it goes past. (-12 health)

choices.text: Hold your ground and shout for the guns

effects.log: You stand fast and roar for the matchlocks, and the two soldiers with the long gun come up, one steadying it on the other's shoulder, and fire. The ball goes nowhere near. The noise does the rest: the tiger turns back into the gongs and the spears. Nobody pays you anything. Nobody dies near you, either.

events.text: {npc} has done the sums. A tiger that eats deer pays nothing; a tiger that eats people pays by the foot; and a tiger seen with a white tail pays more than the whole corps earns in a year, because the court wants white pelts for its thrones. "There is one on the western pass," {npc} says. "It has never taken a person. I could retire on it."

choices.text: Talk {npc} out of it

ok.log: "It keeps the man-eaters off its pass," you say. "Kill it and you will be hunting three where there was one." {npc} thinks for a long time. Then {npc} laughs, the scar pulling. "You do the sums better than me." The white tail stays off the list.

fail.log: {npc} hears you out and goes anyway, with six soldiers. They come back in a month with nothing, and {npc} will not talk about the night at the shrine at the top of the pass, except to say that an old man with a white beard was standing over the bedroll.

choices.text: Go with {npc}, to make sure it goes wrong

effects.log: Three weeks on the western pass. You lose the trail twice on purpose and once by accident. On the last night, at the shrine on the pass, {npc} wakes shouting that an old man with a white beard was standing over the bedroll. You all go home.

choices.text: Go with {npc} for a share

effects.log: Three weeks on the western pass. You never see it. Every morning there are fresh prints round the camp, in a ring, and every night the gong goes missing and is found in the morning hanging in a pine. You come home with nothing and the strong impression that you have been laughed at.

events.text: On the pass between the capital and the firewood villages the woodcutters cross only in tens: they wait at the foot of the road, nine, eight, until the tenth comes, and then go up together behind a gong. Today there are only nine, and it is getting late, and they are all looking at you, because you look as if you could count as two.

choices.text: Make the tenth

effects.log: You take a turn carrying the frame of the oldest one, which he allows with enormous dignity. At the top of the pass every one of them stops, turns, and bows toward a particular rock. You bow too. Nobody explains.

choices.text: Charge them a fee for making the tenth

effects.log: Six taels, grudgingly scraped together. You cross. At the top, as they all bow to a rock, the oldest says without looking at you: "It counts us. It knows who paid." You do not ask what he means.

choices.text: Tell them to wait for morning

effects.log: They wait, grumbling, round a fire at the foot of the road. At midnight a tiger walks along the ridge above the camp, unhurried, and every woodcutter watches it in silence. In the morning they thank you as if you had saved their lives, which you may have.

events.text: Crossing the woodcutters' pass again with a party of ten, and you the tenth. Near the top the gong-beater stops and points: on a ledge above the road a ghost in a torn jacket is standing and counting the party aloud in a pleasant voice, one to ten, and on ten it points at you.

choices.text: Step out of the line and face it

ok.log: "Count again," you tell it. "I am not the tenth. I am two." The ghost frowns, and counts, and gets eleven, and then twelve, because the woodcutters have caught on and are shuffling, and in the end it gives up and sits down on its ledge with its head in its hands. You leave it a rice cake on the way past.

fail.log: You face it, and it calls you by your childhood name in a voice you have not heard for thirty years, and your knees go. The woodcutters drag you over the top by the collar. (-12 health)

choices.text: March the party on, counting backwards at the top of your voices

effects.log: You set ten woodcutters bellowing the numbers backwards from ten, in a muddle, laughing with fright, the whole way down. The ghost loses count somewhere around six and is left on its ledge with its mouth moving, behind you.

events.text: The one who made you everything you are has died, a teacher or the nearest thing to one you ever had, and you have done the old thing that almost nobody does any more: built a straw hut beside the grave and put on coarse hemp, to sit there for three years. It is the first winter. On the first night of snow something huge comes out of the trees, looks at you, and lies down across the doorway of the hut with its back to you and its face to the dark.

choices.text: Share your gruel with it

effects.log: You put half your gruel in the pot lid and push it toward the striped back. It sniffs, looks round over its shoulder at you in pure disbelief, and eats it. After that, every evening, the lid; and every night, the guard.

choices.text: Keep your vigil and pay it no mind

effects.log: You go on with the rites as if it were not there: the morning offering, the evening wailing, the long silence. It stays as if you were not there. Between the two of you, the grave is very well kept.

choices.text: Take up your sword and drive it off

ok.log: It goes, unhurried, as a guest goes when the host is rude. The next night bandits come for the grave goods, and you fight them alone in the snow, and win, and wonder.

fail.log: It does not go. It knocks your sword into the snow with one paw, looks at you with great patience, and lies down again across the door. (-15 health)

events.text: The second winter by the grave. Bandits have heard that a strong master is sitting in a hut on a hill with grave goods and no sleep, and eleven of them come up the slope at the third watch with torches. The tiger across your door stands up.

choices.text: Fight beside it

ok.log: It is the shortest fight of your life. The bandits who can still run, run, and the one at the back is heard shouting that the mourner has a demon. In the morning the tiger is lying across the doorway again, licking a cut, and you dress it with the grave wine, and it lets you.

fail.log: One of them gets a blade into your side before the tiger reaches him. Then nobody is left on the slope who can stand. (-18 health)

choices.text: Stay on your knees at the grave: you swore not to leave it

effects.log: You do not turn your head. You hear the fight in the dark behind you and keep your forehead on the frozen ground. At dawn there are burnt-out torches in the snow, no bandits, and the tiger asleep across your door as if nothing had happened.

events.text: The third year ends. You take off the hemp, burn the hut, and bow to the grave a last time. The tiger that guarded your door for three winters is sitting at the edge of the trees. When you start down the hill it walks beside you to the bottom, and at the road it stops, and you understand that its errand, whatever it was, is finished too.

choices.text: Bow to it as to a fellow mourner

effects.log: You bow. It lowers its great head. Years later you will hear that the old man of the mountain sends his tiger to guard the huts of mourners, and you will think: so that was an errand. It did not feel like one. It felt like company.

choices.text: Ask it to come with you

effects.log: It looks at the road, and at the mountain, and at you, and goes back up the mountain. But for the rest of your life, whenever you are grieving, you dream of a striped back across a doorway, and you sleep.

events.text: The county has begged you to kill the man-eater of the northern ravine: thirty dead in five years, a whole family of charcoal burners among them. You track it to its lair, a cleft full of bones, and it is there, grey and torn-eared and enormous. But on the cliff above it lies a second tiger, with a white tip to its tail, and the two of them have the same face.

choices.text: Kill the man-eater

ok.log: It is a long fight among the bones. When it is done you look up at the cliff. The white-tailed tiger has not moved. It looks down at its dead sibling for a long time, and then at you, and lowers its head once, as if a sentence had been carried out that it could not carry out itself. Then it goes.

fail.deathCause: the man-eater of the northern ravine
fail.log: It is bigger than thirty deaths.

choices.text: Call up to the one on the cliff

effects.log: You call up to it, feeling a fool. It answers, not with words but by coming down and lying between you and the grey one, as an elder lies between a younger sibling and a raised stick. The man-eater slinks off up the ravine. That year the killings stop. The year after, they start again, further north.

events.text: On the anniversary of the northern ravine there is a dead deer laid on your threshold, and the next year, and the next. In the fourth year, nothing; instead, at dusk, a white-tailed tiger sitting in the road outside your gate.

choices.text: Go out and sit in the road with it

effects.log: You sit in the road side by side until dark. It does not want anything. It wanted, you think, somebody who had been there, so that the grief would have a witness. When it goes, it touches its nose to your shoulder, once, like a sibling.

choices.text: Bow from the gate and close it gently

effects.log: It watches the gate close and stays a while longer. In the morning the deer is back on the step, as if to say: very well, then, this way.

events.text: Crossing a western pass at dusk, you hear, ahead in the mist, the voice of the one who raised you calling your childhood name, exactly as it called you in for supper forty years ago. That voice has been in the ground for years. You know what this is: the ghost of somebody a tiger ate, which walks ahead of its tiger calling the next traveller in a voice they cannot refuse. Your feet have already taken three steps toward it.

choices.text: Stop, and answer it with the wrong name

effects.log: "Wrong house," you call back, steadily, and give the name of a neighbour's dog. The voice stops, confused. In the silence you hear something large in the mist behind it sigh, and go away.

choices.text: Follow it with your sword drawn, to find the tiger behind it

ok.log: The ghost leads you to a ledge and the tiger is waiting there, an old grey man-eater with teeth like broken pottery. You kill it. The ghost watches, and when it is over it says, in its own voice, "Thank you," and is not there any more.

fail.deathCause: a ghost on the western pass, calling in a beloved voice
fail.log: It was the voice you could not refuse.

choices.text: Ask the ghost its own name

ok.log: The voice stops. In the mist a figure in a torn white jacket turns round, and it is nobody you know: a young porter, surprised. "Nobody asks," it says, in its own voice. It tells you its name, and its village. Then it walks away from the pass into the trees, as if it had remembered somewhere it had to be.

fail.log: It does not answer. It only calls again, closer, in that voice, and you have to bite your own hand to stop walking. (-8 health)

events.text: The porter's village, three valleys over. You find the house, and an old woman who was the porter's younger sister and has waited sixty years to know where her brother went. Nobody ever found him. There was nothing to bury.

choices.text: Take her up to the pass and build a cairn together

effects.log: The two of you carry stones for three days. She brings a steamer pot from her own kitchen and turns it over on the cairn, and you drive an iron spindle through its hole the old way, so the dead cannot wander; and then she does a thing the old way does not say. She pulls the spindle out again. "He can come home now," she says. "The door is open." That night, in her village, a dog barks for joy at an empty gate.

choices.text: Tell her he is at peace

effects.log: You tell her he asked after the village. It is almost true. She nods for a long time, and then gets up and sets a second bowl of rice at the evening table, and leaves it there.

events.text: A tiger has taken a woodcutter on the mountain above the village, and the village is holding the tiger-death funeral: what was left is burned where it fell, a cairn raised over the ash, an earthenware steamer pot turned upside down on the cairn, and an iron spindle from a spinning wheel driven through the hole in its bottom. {npc}, the shaman, explains it as the bells ring: the pot is a fortress, the hole is heaven, the spindle is lightning, and the ghost inside goes round like a wheel and can never get out to lure anyone else. The village has asked you to guard the cairn the first night, because the tiger comes back for its ghost.

choices.text: Guard the cairn through the night

ok.log: It comes at the third watch, a lean young tiger with blood on its muzzle, and circles the cairn, and circles you. You do not move. At dawn it goes, and you understand that it was not after the ghost at all: it was trying to see what it had done.

fail.log: It comes at the third watch and you are not fast enough. But it does not touch the pot. It only stands over it for a long time, and goes. (-15 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} what becomes of the ghost

effects.log: "It goes round," {npc} says. "For ever. Like thread." The bells stop. "It is a cruel thing to do to somebody who was only unlucky. But a ghost on the loose takes the next one, and the next. The village chooses the living." {npc} looks at the pot. "I always hope the tiger lays them to rest itself. Some do."

events.text: Passing the old cairn on the mountain years later, you find the steamer pot set neatly beside it, the right way up, with the iron spindle laid across it, and on the cairn a ring of tiger prints going round and round in the frost, as if something had circled it all night and then, at dawn, carefully lifted the lid.

choices.text: Put the pot back and drive the spindle home

effects.log: You do it, because the village asked you to once. The next morning the pot is off again and the spindle laid across it, as neatly as before. You leave it after that. Some arguments are not yours.

choices.text: Leave it open

effects.log: You leave it. Some tigers lay their ghosts to rest themselves, the shaman said. You stand there a long time hoping this one was one of them, and then you walk on, lighter.

events.text: A new king has asked the mountain god to clear the tigers from the hills around the new capital and send them north across the great river, and you have been sent with the escort: three hundred soldiers to walk behind a column of tigers to the ice and see them over. It is the strangest march of your life. The tigers walk in a line like monks. At the last ridge before the river, one of them, a tigress heavy with cubs, lies down in the snow and will not get up, looking back at the granite mountain they have left.

choices.text: Hide her in the rocks and say nothing

effects.log: You drop back with a sack of millet you claim needs mending, and wait until the column is over the ridge, and lead her into a cleft in the granite. She looks at you with eyes like lamps. When the escort is counted at the river, there is one tiger fewer, and nobody in the line of soldiers says a word.

choices.text: Report her to the officer

effects.log: The officer looks at her, and at the river, and at the sky, where an old man with a white beard is standing on a cloud, very still, watching. The officer clears his throat and says that he counted wrong. The column goes on without her.

choices.text: Ask the mountain god, aloud, to let her stay

ok.log: You shout it at the sky, in front of three hundred soldiers. There is a long silence. Then the snow on the ridge in front of her parts in a path leading back toward the granite mountain, and she gets up and walks it. Her cubs, you hear later, filled that mountain, and the capital has had tigers on its doorstep ever since.

fail.log: The sky says nothing. But at dawn, when the column goes down to the ice, the tigress is gone from the ridge, and there is only one set of prints, going back.

events.text: Years after the march to the river, you are passing the granite mountain outside the capital where you hid a tigress, and the woodcutters at the foot of the pass are waiting in tens, and grumbling about the tigers on the mountain, which they say are the boldest in the country and know every woodcutter by name.

choices.text: Cross alone, at dusk, to see

effects.log: Halfway up, on a rock, three young tigers are sitting in a row, watching you come. They do not move. As you pass, the middle one yawns, and you would swear, from the set of its head, that it knows exactly who you are.

choices.text: Make the tenth for the woodcutters, and keep quiet

effects.log: You go up with them behind the gong. At the top the oldest woodcutter says, to nobody, that the tigers here were let stay by a soldier once. "A fool," he says, comfortably. "Bless them."

events.text: The spring festival of the second month: the whole town circles the old stone pagoda all night with lanterns, round and round, praying for the year, the way the young people of Silla did in the old story. You have been circling for hours. So has {npc}, a stranger in white who has kept pace beside you since the first lantern was lit, who smells faintly of pine and snow, and whose eyes catch the lamplight the way a cat's do.

choices.text: Speak to {npc}

effects.log: "You walk well," {npc} says, "for somebody on two feet." It is a strange compliment. You walk together till dawn and talk about nothing, and laugh, and at first light {npc} is gone between one step and the next, and you are left circling alone.

choices.text: Keep circling in silence beside {npc}

effects.log: Round and round, side by side, not a word. Near dawn {npc} matches your breathing, and you match {npc}'s, and the whole courtyard seems to breathe with you. Then the bell for morning rings and {npc} is gone.

choices.text: Look at {npc}'s shadow on the pagoda stones

ok.log: In the lantern light, on the stones, your shadow is a person. {npc}'s shadow has four feet and a long tail. {npc} sees you see it, and does not run, which is the bravest thing you have ever watched anyone do.

fail.log: Only a shadow. You feel foolish. {npc} is smiling at you as if you had done something sweet.

events.text: {npc}, the stranger from the pagoda, comes to find you a year later, afraid. "I have three siblings," {npc} says. "Older, and crueller, and they have eaten people. Heaven has decided that one of us must die for it. A blade is coming, and the blade is somebody strong." {npc} looks at you for a long time. "It is you. Heaven has chosen you."

choices.text: Refuse heaven's commission, whatever heaven says

effects.log: You burn the summons that came the next morning. Heaven, it turns out, has other blades. In the autumn you hear that three tigers were killed on the northern mountain in one night, and that a fourth, smaller, was seen at dawn at the pagoda, alone, circling.

choices.text: Go after the three man-eaters, and only them

ok.log: Three nights, three tigers, each bigger than the last. When it is done heaven's sentence is more than carried out, and {npc} is alive, and will not look at you, because they were family. Both things stay true for a long time.

fail.log: Two of them nearly kill you in a ravine. {npc} drags you out by the collar, in a shape that is not a person's. (-25 health)

choices.text: Promise {npc} you will find another way

effects.log: "There is no other way in the story," {npc} says. "In the story I give you my life on your blade and you build me a temple." You say the story can change. {npc} laughs, and touches your hand, and is gone, and you never learn which ending heaven chose.

events.text: You have built a small temple at the foot of the hill where the old pagoda stands, as the young hwarang did in the story, though you could not quite say for whom. On its first spring night somebody circles the pagoda alone with a lantern, in white, and when you go out they are gone, and on the stones in the lantern light are the prints of four feet.

choices.text: Name it the Temple the Tiger Wished For

effects.log: The monks think it a strange name. Pilgrims love it. Every spring after that, on the festival night, one lantern circles the pagoda that nobody is carrying.

choices.text: Circle the pagoda every spring for the rest of your life

effects.log: Every second month, all night, round and round. Some years you are alone. Some years there is somebody in white beside you who smells of pine and snow and says nothing. You never ask which kind of year it will be.

events.text: {npc}, a shaman from the river villages, has come with an odd request. A white-tailed tiger has been seen at the shrine on the western pass, night after night, lying beside the old tiger-death cairns as if keeping watch over them. {npc} believes it wants its ghosts laid to rest and cannot do it alone, and has asked the mountain for help. "The mountain sent me a dream of you," {npc} says. "I do not know why. You are not a shaman. You are very loud."

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the pass

effects.log: "Bring rice cakes," {npc} says, "and a lantern, and your loudness. The dead are hard of hearing."

choices.text: Ask what the rite needs from you

effects.log: "Hands," {npc} says. "Each ghost must be walked to the edge of the pass by somebody alive, and let go of. I have only two hands, and there are four of them." {npc} considers you. "Five, if you count the tiger."

events.text: Night on the western pass. {npc} rings the bells and sings the long song for the dead of the road, and one by one, out of the old cairns, the ghosts stand up: a porter, two woodcutters, a girl with a basket. On the rock above the road the white-tailed tiger lies with its head on its paws, watching each one with an expression you would call shame in a person.

choices.text: Walk them to the edge of the pass, one by one

effects.log: Four cold hands, one after another. Each ghost stops at the edge of the pass and looks back at the tiger on the rock, and the tiger lowers its head to each. Then they go. When the fourth is gone the tiger stands and says, in a voice like stones settling, "Ask my name." {npc} does, and it answers, and {npc} writes it on the shrine wall.

choices.text: Tell the tiger to walk them itself

ok.log: You climb to the rock, carefully, and tell it this is not your work. It looks at you for a long time. Then it comes down and walks each ghost to the edge itself, slow as a funeral, and the ghosts are not afraid of it at all, which seems to undo it more than anything.
