fail.log: It does not like being told. A paw sends you down the slope. But when you climb back up, it is walking the first ghost to the edge, stiffly, without looking at you. (-10 health)

events.text: {npc}, a minister of the court, has come with an iron cage on an ox cart and a great deal of silver. "A white tiger appears only when the ruler is virtuous," {npc} says. "There is one in the western mountains. The king's enemies say the reign is cursed. We need it brought in alive and shown in the palace yard. As proof, you understand."

choices.text: Take the commission

effects.log: Two hundred taels in advance, and the ox cart, and a clerk to keep the accounts. {npc} bows. The cage, empty, rattles behind you all the way to the western mountains like a laugh.

choices.text: Refuse: an omen in a cage proves the opposite

effects.log: "A white tiger that comes because the ruler is virtuous," you say, "does not come in a cage." {npc} goes red, then white, then thoughtful. The cage goes back to the capital empty, and you hear later that the minister repeated your sentence to the king, who laughed.

choices.text: Take it, and go to warn the tiger

effects.log: Two hundred taels. You take the cage west anyway, because it is the fastest way to reach the tiger before anybody else does.

events.text: The western mountains in winter. You find the white tiger at a frozen spring, lying in snow so white that it is only a shape where the snow is warmer. It lifts its head and looks at you, and at the cage on the ox cart far below in the valley, and says, in a human voice: "I know what that is for."

choices.text: Try to take it anyway

ok.log: It does not fight as hard as it could. Only on the road to the capital do you understand that it came quietly because it wanted to see the king. In the palace yard it looks at the king through the bars for a long time, and the king looks back. In the morning the cage is open, its bars bent outward like grass, and the king has pardoned every prisoner in the capital.

fail.deathCause: the white tiger of the western mountains, hunted for a court's proof
fail.log: Virtue does not come in a cage.

choices.text: Ask it what it wants you to do

effects.log: "Go back," it says, "and tell your minister that the white tiger came to the edge of the forest, looked at the cage, and laughed. That is the true omen. A virtuous king will understand it." You do. The king does.

choices.text: Unhitch the ox and break the cage

effects.log: It takes you an afternoon with a stone. The ox wanders off, delighted. The tiger watches the whole thing from the spring with its chin on its paws, and when the last bar is down it gets up, stretches, and walks away into the snow, its tail swinging like a banner.

events.text: {npc}, an alchemist of a great sect, has a recipe for the Tiger Bone Elixir in its old form: the bones of a tiger five hundred years old, steeped forty days in wine with deer antler and ginseng, which gives the drinker, the recipe says, a tiger's bones. "The old ones whiten at five hundred," {npc} says. "I have found one. I need a hunter who will not be frightened by what it says to you before it dies."

choices.text: Accept the hunt

effects.log: A hundred taels and a map of the western mountains. {npc} pours you a cup of something dark and bitter: tea, left to stand too long. "It will talk," {npc} says. "They always do, the old ones. Do not listen."

choices.text: Ask to read the recipe first

ok.log: At the bottom of the old paper, in another hand: THE BONES REMEMBER. OF THREE WHO DRANK IT, TWO WOKE ON ALL FOURS. {npc} sees you read it and does not blink.

fail.log: {npc} rolls the recipe up before you have read half. "Trade secret," {npc} says, smiling. You leave without the commission, and with a bad taste in your mouth.

choices.text: Refuse and leave

effects.log: {npc} bows. "Someone will say yes," {npc} says. On the road home you find you are walking west, faster and faster, without being sure why.

events.text: Since the alchemist, you dream of being steeped: forty days in a bronze cauldron under a low fire, the lid on, and a voice outside the cauldron saying, kindly, "It is only medicine." You wake each morning with your bones aching as if they belonged to somebody else.

choices.text: Go back and break the cauldron

ok.log: You walk into the sect's furnace hall at midnight and put your fist through the bronze. The bones in it, steeped white, roll out across the floor, and every one of them is warm. You carry them west in a sack and bury them under a pine on the pass, and the dreams stop.

fail.log: The sect's disciples throw you out before you reach the cauldron. But the alchemist, you hear, never finishes the steeping: on the thirty-ninth day the fire would not stay lit. (-15 health)

choices.text: Ride west and warn the white tiger

effects.log: You find the pass and sit on the road until something huge sits down on the rock above you. You tell it about the cauldron. "I know," it says. "My grandmother is in it. Thank you for coming anyway." It sounds, for a tiger, very tired, and grateful.

events.text: The court has given you the right wing of the western army, and with it a banner that has not been unfurled in forty years: a white tiger on white silk, worked in silver thread, which flies on the right of every royal procession and before every campaign in the west. The northern horsemen are over the river. On the first night of the march the banner bearer comes to your tent, pale. "The tiger on the banner," he says. "It turned its head."

choices.text: Go and look

effects.log: By torchlight the silver tiger is exactly as it was embroidered, head forward, mouth open. You are turning away when its eye catches the light and follows you. You tell the banner bearer it was the wind. Neither of you believes it, and both of you sleep better.

choices.text: Tell him it was the wind, and believe it yourself

effects.log: He goes, unconvinced. In the morning, when the banner is raised at the head of the right wing, the whole wing sees the silver tiger turn its head toward the north, and nobody needs telling what that means.

events.text: Battle on the dry plain. The northern horsemen come in at the right wing, your wing, in a white storm of dust, riding under their own white star, the Hairy Head: the star of the northern riders, and of mourning clothes. In the dust, for one moment, your banner is not silk. It is a tiger running ahead of your line, and it looks back at you as if to ask who should run and who should die.

choices.text: Break them, but let them run

ok.log: You break the charge and open your line on the left and let them through it, running north. Your officers call it madness. A year later the horsemen send envoys instead of riders, because the ones who ran home told their families about the tiger that let them go.

fail.log: The charge hits harder than you planned and you are unhorsed in the dust. The line holds. The horsemen run anyway, and you let them, from the ground, with a broken arm. (-20 health)

choices.text: No quarter: the west must be safe for a generation

ok.log: None of them reach the river. The west is safe for years. That winter every village north of the river wears mourning white, and the silver tiger on your banner, when you look at it, has its eyes shut.

fail.deathCause: the northern horsemen, under the white tiger banner
fail.log: The Hairy Head is a star of mourning clothes.

choices.text: Hold the line, and let the tiger choose

effects.log: You hold. You do not pursue. You watch the tiger in the dust run along the horsemen's front, and wherever it looks, men turn back; wherever it does not, they come on and die. At the end of the day you do not know whether you commanded the battle or only witnessed a verdict.

events.text: The war is over. The white tiger banner is to be returned to the palace storehouse and folded away for another forty years. When the keepers unroll it to count the stitches, the silver thread has turned white all over, as a tiger's coat whitens in its five-hundredth year, and on the silk there are tiny brown stains along the tiger's flank, the colour of old blood, that no washer can lift.

choices.text: Ask to keep it in your own house

ok.log: The keepers refuse, then hesitate, then give in, because none of them wants to sleep in the same storehouse as it. It hangs in your hall for the rest of your life, and no thief ever comes through your gate.

fail.log: The keepers fold it away. On the night it goes into the storehouse you dream of a tiger lying down in the dark to sleep for years, and are glad for it.

choices.text: Burn incense before it, and let it go

effects.log: One stick of incense, a bow, and the keepers fold it away. The smoke goes west, all of it, though there is no wind.

events.text: The first month. A tiger has walked into the rear garden of the palace, through two walls and a gate, and is lying under the pines by the frozen lotus pond as if it owned them. The ministers are in uproar: one faction says a tiger in the garden means yin strong and yang weak, a bad omen for the throne; another says it is the guardian of the west come to look at the king. {npc}, the chief minister, has asked you, as the strongest person at court, to go out and settle the question one way or the other.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Go out and sit with it under the pines

effects.log: You sit down a body-length from it in the snow. After a while it says, without turning its head: "I came to see whether the king would come out in person. Go and tell the king that." You go back to the ministers with snow on your robe and a message nobody wants to carry.

choices.text: Drive it out of the palace

ok.log: It goes, over the wall, unhurried. The ministers who said it was a bad omen are delighted. The ones who said it was a guardian go quiet, and stay quiet, and that spring the king falls ill.

fail.log: It does not go. You end up in the frozen pond, through the ice, and the tiger watches you climb out with an expression the court painters spend the next year trying to capture. (-20 health)

choices.text: Tell {npc} the omen means whatever the king does next

effects.log: {npc} stares at you. Then, slowly, {npc} begins to smile, and goes in to the king with that sentence and nothing else.

events.text: The king has come out into the snow, bareheaded, against the advice of every minister, and is standing in front of the tiger under the pines. You are beside him, ready. The tiger looks at the king for a long time without moving. The king glances at you.
events.arc: The Tiger in the Palace Garden

choices.text: Murmur to the king to bow

effects.log: The king bows to a tiger in his own garden, in front of the whole court. The tiger rises, bows back, as deep, and walks out through the gate it came in by. The court historians argue for a month about how to write it down. In the end they write: the guardian of the west came, and was received.

choices.text: Murmur to the king to ask it a question

effects.log: The king asks it, in a voice that only shakes a little, whether his reign is just. The tiger says, "Not yet," and leaves. It is the best thing that ever happens to that reign.

events.text: You have been asked to judge a case no magistrate in the province will touch: {npc}, a farmer, killed the tax collector who took the village's seed rice in a famine year. Every word of it is admitted. The law says death. The village says the collector killed thirty by taking the seed. It is autumn. On the night before the verdict you go out into the yard, look west at the three straight stars of the Balance, and say aloud, to no one, that you cannot do this.

choices.text: Wait for an answer

effects.log: Something answers. Behind you in the yard a white tiger the size of the courthouse is sitting with its stripes made of night sky. "Nor can I," it says, "every year. Shall we hear it together?"

choices.text: Decide alone, as a judge must

effects.log: You go back in and sit up with the papers until dawn, and give a verdict, and live with it. In the yard, the stars of the Balance are very level, and you take that, without knowing why, as a kindness.

events.text: The verdict. {npc} kneels in the yard. Behind your bench, unseen by anyone else, the tiger of stars sits like a second judge, and as you weigh each fact the three stars in its chest tip, a little this way, a little that. "A capital case," it murmurs. "Under the Three Stars. Mercy has a price and so has severity. Choose, and I will file it."

choices.text: Death, as the law says, and the village's debt forgiven

effects.log: {npc} hears it without flinching, and bows to you. The village weeps and pays no tax for three years. Behind you the tiger says, very quietly, "Severity, and justly. Entered." You do not sleep that night or the next.

choices.text: Exile, and the collector's office torn down

effects.log: {npc} goes north with a bundle and a letter of yours to a magistrate you trust. The collector's office is pulled down by the village, stone by stone, in a day. "Level," the tiger says. "Entered." It sounds, for a moment, proud of you.

choices.text: Pardon: the famine was the murderer

ok.log: You argue it so well that the provincial governor, who came to watch you fail, goes away and rewrites the famine laws. {npc} goes home to plant the next year's rice. "Mercy," the tiger says. "Justly. Entered." In its chest the three stars hang perfectly level.

fail.log: You pardon {npc}, and the governor overturns you within the month, and the sentence is carried out by somebody else. "Mercy," the tiger says, "unjustly argued. Not entered." It does not say it unkindly.

events.text: {npc} is to be executed at dawn for a murder you are nearly certain {he} did not do. The law is old: no execution on a solar term, none in rain, none before first light. Tomorrow is not a solar term. The sky is clear. You have one night. On the prison roof, as you stand at the bars, a white tiger is sitting very still, looking up at the cloudless sky.

choices.text: Ask the tiger for rain

ok.log: "Rain is not mine," it says. "It belongs to the dragon of the left ridge, and we quarrel about it." It looks at you a long time. "But I will ask." At the fourth watch, out of a clear sky, it rains, softly, from the east, and the execution is put off a day, and in that day you find the real killer.

fail.log: "Rain is not mine," it says, "and I do not ask favours of the east." It goes. You spend the rest of the night running, and do not find enough.

choices.text: Spend the night finding the real killer

ok.log: A pawnbroker's ledger, a knife sold twice, a widow who lied for a reason. At first light you walk into the magistrate's hall with the proof and {npc} walks out of the cangue. On the roof, the tiger is gone, and the frost on the tiles is melted in the shape of somebody who sat there all night, waiting to see what you would do.

fail.log: You run all night and find half of it. Half is enough to delay, not to free. The magistrate gives you three days, grudgingly. (-10 health)

choices.text: Break {npc} out

ok.log: The cangue splits, the wall comes down, and {npc} is gone into the dark. You are a fugitive from the law for a year until the truth comes out. On the night you break the wall, the tiger on the roof watches, and says only, "Severe, to the law. Merciful, to the person. Both are entered."

fail.log: The guards are many and wide awake. You are thrown out of the prison yard, and {npc} is still inside. (-15 health)

events.text: Every autumn since the night of the rain from a clear sky, the magistrates of the county have kept a new custom nobody can explain: before any execution they send a clerk to look west at dusk, and if the three straight stars of the Balance are not level, the sentence waits a day.

choices.text: Ask the clerks whether they have ever waited

effects.log: "Four times," the oldest clerk says. "Every time, something turned up in the extra day." He shrugs. "We do not ask questions about it. The stars are very patient with us."

choices.text: Look west yourself at dusk

effects.log: Three stars in a row, level as a carpenter's rule. Below them, in the dusk, the faint shape of a great white head turned toward the county. You bow, and it does not bow back, because it is working.

events.text: Heaven has sent executioners for the White Tiger of the western mountain. Its verdicts, somebody in the Jade Court has decided, have grown too severe, and a guardian who judges must itself be judged. They come down the sky at dusk in armour like frost, carrying long-handled axes, and the tiger is lying on its peak with its head on its paws, and it is not getting up.

choices.text: Stand in front of it

ok.log: The first axe comes down on your guard and rings like a temple bell. And the second. By the ninth your arms are numb to the shoulder and heaven's executioners are looking at one another. The tenth does not come. Their captain lowers the axe and says, "It has a witness. The case is reopened." They go back up the sky.

fail.deathCause: heaven's executioners, standing before the White Tiger
fail.log: Heaven's axes are heavier than any you have known.

choices.text: Demand to see the charge

ok.log: The executioners' captain, astonished to be asked, unrolls it. You read it aloud on the peak. Of the eleven verdicts listed, three were too severe and eight were exactly right, and two of the eight had saved the very official who drafted the charge. The captain rolls it up again very slowly.

fail.log: The captain does not answer you. An axe-handle sends you down the slope. But the asking delayed them an hour, and an hour, on a mountain, is when the clouds come in. (-12 health)

choices.text: Ask the tiger whether the charge is true

effects.log: "Some of it," it says, without lifting its head. "I punished three who should have been pardoned. I would like them to know I know." You carry that answer up the sky yourself, to the Jade Court, and it is the answer that stays the axe.

events.text: A clerk of heaven, {npc}, comes to you with a scroll and an expression of great weariness. "You interfered with heaven's sentence on the White Tiger of the west," {npc} says. "The Jade Court would like to know why. Briefly. In writing."

choices.text: Write it: a judge who can be wrong must be judged by one who can be wrong too

effects.log: You write two pages. {npc} reads them twice and rolls up the scroll. "That will annoy several people," {npc} says, with the first sign of pleasure you have seen. "Good."

choices.text: Refuse to write anything

effects.log: {npc} sighs. "This goes on your record," {npc} says. "Every life." You say that is fine. {npc} writes it down. It does.

events.text: You have come to the western mountains for the one opponent left in the world worth the walk: the Tiger of Autumn, which breathes out, they say, and the leaves fall. It is waiting for you on a plateau among the maples. When it breathes out every leaf on the mountain comes down at once, red and gold, and in the storm of leaves it is everywhere at once.

choices.text: Fight it with everything you have

ok.log: For a day and a night you fight in a storm of leaves. At dawn you are standing and so is it, and the mountain is bare. It sits down. So do you. "Good," it says. "Again in a hundred years." You both know you will not have a hundred years. It says it anyway, as a courtesy.

fail.deathCause: the Tiger of Autumn, in a duel among the falling leaves
fail.log: Every leaf falls in autumn.

choices.text: Fight it with nothing: stand in the leaves and breathe

ok.log: You do not strike. You stand in the falling leaves and breathe as it breathes, out when it breathes out, and after an hour the leaves fall around you and not on you. It stops. "That," it says, "is the only way anyone has ever beaten me." You are not sure you beat anything. You leave with autumn in your lungs.

fail.log: You try to breathe with it and lose the rhythm, and the leaves cut like knives. It stops before it has to. "Close," it says. (-15 health)

choices.text: Bow, and ask instead to watch it hunt

effects.log: It considers this, and seems flattered. For a season you follow it through the western mountains at a respectful distance and learn more about patience than forty years of practice could teach. It never once lets you see the kill. "That part is not for watching," it says.

events.text: Years after the plateau of maples, in your own courtyard, you breathe out at dusk without thinking, a long breath with something of metal in it, and the persimmon tree drops every leaf.

choices.text: Practise it until you can choose which leaves

effects.log: It takes you a year. Then one autumn evening you breathe out, and one red leaf falls from the top of the persimmon, and only that one, turning slowly all the way down. Far off in the west, something very large laughs.

choices.text: Never do it again: it is not yours

effects.log: You sweep up the leaves and do not do it again. But every autumn after that, the first frost comes to your courtyard a day before anywhere else, as if somebody were keeping a promise for you.

events.text: A magpie lands on your gate and does not chatter. It speaks: "The White Tiger of the west is to take the Western Seat at the autumn equinox. The Four Guardians need a human witness strong enough to stand the sight. You have been named."

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: The magpie bows, which looks ridiculous, and flies west. You spend the summer wondering what a human is supposed to wear to the seating of a constellation.

choices.text: Ask why a human is needed

effects.log: "Because the west is where humans harvest," the magpie says. "Its guardian is seated in front of somebody who has carried a sheaf. It has always been so." It looks you over. "You have carried a sheaf?" You have.

events.text: The autumn equinox. From the highest peak in the west you watch the White Tiger climb a stair of cloud toward seven stars that have arranged themselves into an empty seat. Halfway up it stops, turns its head, and looks down at you. Every witness, it seems, is asked one question. "Was I just?"

choices.text: Answer honestly, whatever the answer is

effects.log: You tell it the truth, the just and the not so just. It listens to the end. Then it goes up and takes the seat, and the seven stars blaze, and the harvest in the west that year is the best in living memory, and the first thing it does as Guardian of the West is breathe out, gently, so that the leaves on your peak fall around you like a blessing.

choices.text: Tell it that asking is the answer

effects.log: It laughs, a sound like a landslide in autumn. "A clever witness," it says. "Good. I was afraid of a flatterer." It goes up into its seat. On the west wall of every tomb painted after that year, the painters swear, the tiger's mouth is open in something that looks very like a grin.

events.text: Meditating on a western peak at the autumn equinox, you feel the season turn in your lungs: something cold and bright, like the taste of a new blade, coming in on the west wind. Under it, very far off, something huge is breathing in time with the year.

choices.text: Breathe with it

ok.log: In, with the far breath; out, with it. On the third breath every leaf in the valley below lets go at once, red and gold, and comes down in a single long sigh. You have breathed autumn. Your qi comes back to you heavier and cleaner, like ore that has been through the fire.

fail.log: You lose the rhythm on the second breath and cough like a novice. The far breathing goes on without you, patiently, the way a teacher waits.

choices.text: Stop, and listen only

effects.log: You listen until dark. It is the sound of the harvest being weighed: every field, every granary, every account in the west, all at once, on a beam held level by something with a very steady paw.

events.text: A disciple of yours, overproud, has started a fight that could become a sect war, and every elder is waiting to see what you will do. It is autumn. You can feel the metal in the west wind.

choices.text: Breathe once over the disciple, and let the leaves fall

effects.log: You breathe out over the courtyard. Every leaf on every tree in the sect comes down in one breath, and the disciple, standing in the sudden rain of them, understands without a word being said that a season can end. The war does not happen.

choices.text: Judge the quarrel properly, both sides heard

ok.log: Three days of hearing both sides. Your verdict pleases nobody completely, which, the elders agree, is how you know it was right. That night the stars of the Balance hang very level over the sect.

fail.log: You hear both sides and still cannot see it. You say so. The elders are disappointed, then, slowly, impressed. The quarrel cools on its own while everyone waits for you.

events.text: In the Upper Realm a road runs west to seven halls of white stone, each lit by one star: Legs, Bond, Stomach, Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak, Three Stars. From far off the seven halls together are a tiger. {npc}, the keeper of the first, an old official with a white beard and a ledger, bows. "Each hall holds one case," {npc} says. "Water, a mob, a granary, a funeral, a hunt, an army, a death. The tiger that owns these halls has judged ten thousand of each. Would you like to judge one of each, and see?"
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the West

choices.text: Walk the seven halls

ok.log: It takes you seven years. In the Hall of Legs two villages want one ditch. In the Hall of Bond a crowd wants a hanging. In the Stomach, a magistrate sits on a full granary in a famine. In the Hairy Head a widow will not take off the mourning white. In the Net, a hunter killed a tiger that had killed no one. In the Turtle Beak, a deserter. In the Three Stars, a murderer who did it for a mother. You judge each, and the keeper writes each down, and at the end you are lighter and older and very tired.

fail.log: You get through the Legs and the Bond and stall in the Stomach, where you cannot make the magistrate open the granary without becoming a tyrant yourself. {npc} brings you tea every morning for a year and says nothing. You leave knowing that a granary is harder than a sword.

choices.text: Ask {npc} which hall is hardest

effects.log: "Everyone thinks it is the Three Stars," {npc} says. "The capital cases. It is not. It is the Bond: the crowd. A crowd is right and wrong at the same time, and very loud." {npc} laughs at your face.

events.text: The keeper of the Hall of Legs finds you again. "The White Tiger read your seven verdicts," {npc} says. "It disagrees with two of them. It would like to argue. It does not argue with many people."
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the West

choices.text: Go and argue

effects.log: It comes down out of its seven stars and lies across the road like a river of frost, and you argue for a month about a ditch and a deserter. You lose one argument and win the other. At the end it touches its nose to your forehead and says, "Now there are two of us who know."

choices.text: Concede both: it has judged ten thousand

effects.log: {npc} carries your answer in. It comes back with a reply on a white leaf: Ten thousand, and some of them wrong. Come and argue. You go, the next autumn.

events.text: At the end of the seventh hall there is a door you did not see the first time, and behind it a small room with a plain bench and a set of scales on a stand: the Balance itself, the three stars of it no bigger than lamp flames. One pan has a white feather in it. The other is empty, and it is level.
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the West

choices.text: Put something of your own in the empty pan

effects.log: You put in the first thing your hand finds: a grain of rice from the world below, carried up in a fold of your sleeve for a thousand years. The beam does not move. A feather and a grain weigh the same, here. You sit on the plain bench until you understand why, which takes a decade, and is worth it.

choices.text: Leave it level, and close the door softly

effects.log: You close the door. Behind it, very faintly, the beam creaks once, as if somebody had sighed with relief that you did not touch it.

events.text: You are summoned to the hall of the Four Guardians. The White Tiger's record is being read: its docket, its ghosts, its balance. On the east side a long stormcloud lies across the Azure Dragon's seat; the Vermilion Bird is on the south, the Black Tortoise and its snake on the north, and in the centre the Yellow Dragon presides. "You lived below," the Yellow Dragon says. "In a valley between two ridges, a tiger held the right one. Was it a good guardian? Testify."

choices.text: Testify to its mercy

effects.log: You tell them about children carried home through the night and mourners guarded for three winters. The Vermilion Bird sings one note. The Tortoise writes. The White Tiger looks at the floor, which in a tiger is embarrassment, and counts in its favour.

choices.text: Testify to its severity

effects.log: You tell them about cairns on the pass and a pot with a spindle through it and verdicts that should have been pardons. The stormcloud on the east side rumbles agreement. The White Tiger does not look away from you once. When you finish, it bows to you, the deepest bow in the hall.

choices.text: Testify to both, plainly

ok.log: Mercy and severity, side by side, without softening either. The hall is silent. The Yellow Dragon says, "The beam is level, then." The record is closed. The White Tiger keeps its seat, and as you leave it says, very low, "Thank you for not lying in my favour."

fail.log: You try to say both and manage neither. The Black Tortoise writes "inconclusive". The White Tiger catches your eye and, very slightly, twitches its tail.

events.text: The Azure Dragon of the East finds you alone in a cloud garden of the Upper Realm. "You testified for the tiger of the right ridge," it says. "We quarrelled about the rain for three hundred years. I want to know something. Did it ever speak of me?"

choices.text: Tell it the tiger called it what was coming

effects.log: "Left ridge," the Dragon repeats. "So. You are what was coming." It laughs, a sound like spring ice breaking. "Yes. It said that the first time. It was the most welcome I have ever had." It drifts away east, still laughing.

choices.text: Tell it the tiger never once complained of it to you

effects.log: The Dragon is quiet a long time. "That is like it," it says at last. "It complained only to my face." It sounds, for a dragon, almost tender.

events.text: The White Emperor of the West, who was once a tiger and is now autumn itself, asks for an audience. There is a world below the Upper Realm, it says, where the fields grow green for ever and never ripen: no autumn, no harvest, no reckoning, and its people are hungry in the middle of plenty. "I cannot go," the Emperor says. "If I leave the west, the west forgets to fall. You are a sovereign. You could carry an autumn there."

choices.text: Carry it

effects.log: It puts a single red leaf in your palm, cold as a coin. You carry it down for a hundred years. Where you set it on the green world, the green turns gold from that spot outward, field by field, and somewhere a farmer who has never seen a harvest drops a sickle in astonishment and then picks it up again.

choices.text: Ask the White Emperor what it was like to be a tiger

effects.log: "Hungry," the Emperor says. "Always. And there was a pass, at the very beginning, and a human who threw me a rice cake, or called me kin, or only stood still." It smiles. "I think about that human more than about my whole reign."

choices.text: Decline: a sovereign has a world of their own to keep

effects.log: The Emperor bows, unoffended. "That is the right answer for a sovereign," it says, "and the wrong one for a farmer." It sends someone else. From far off you watch the green world, and see it, after a long while, turn faintly gold.

events.text: The world you carried autumn to has had its first harvest, and its people have done what people do: they have invented a festival, and built a little shrine of stones at the top of a pass, and painted on a plank inside it an old person with a white beard and, at their knee, a striped animal they have never seen, drawn from a dream.

choices.text: Go down and look at the painting

effects.log: It is badly drawn and entirely right. The animal at the old person's knee has a white tip to its tail. You stand in front of it for a long time with the strange feeling that a whole long story has just started again, somewhere you cannot see.

choices.text: Leave a rice cake on the rock above the pass

effects.log: One rice cake, wrapped in a leaf, on a flat rock above a road. In the morning it is gone. Nothing on this world eats rice cakes. You go back up to the Upper Realm very quietly, smiling.

events.text: The woman who raised you is very ill, and the physician's medicine is in the town on the far side of the mountain, and nobody will cross the mountain at night. You go anyway, with the jar in a cloth and your heart going like a drum. On the way back, at the top, in the dark, your legs stop working. Something warm and enormous lies down in the snow in front of you, with its back to you, and waits.

choices.text: Climb on

effects.log: Its fur is warm and smells of pine and frost. You hold on with one hand and keep the jar safe with the other, and somewhere in the forest you fall asleep. You wake at your own gate at dawn with the jar unbroken. She lives. All your life, nobody believes you, and all your life it does not matter.

choices.text: Ask it, out loud, if it will eat you

effects.log: It turns its head and looks at you over its shoulder, the way the old people look at a child who has asked a silly question. Then it waits some more. You climb on. You are home before dawn.

events.text: Grown and strong, you are crossing a mountain at night when you come on a child sitting in the snow at the top, with a jar of medicine in a cloth, legs gone, too frightened to cry. You remember a warm back and a smell of pine and frost.

choices.text: Carry the child down yourself

effects.log: You carry the child on your back down the dark side of the mountain. Halfway, the child falls asleep, and you notice that something huge is walking a little way off among the trees, keeping pace, not interfering, the way an old teacher watches a student do a thing correctly at last.

choices.text: Sit with the child, and wait to see who comes

effects.log: You wait. It comes: the same back, older, whiter at the tail. It looks at you a long time, and at the child, and lies down in the snow. You put the child on its back and walk beside it all the way down, with your hand on its shoulder.

events.text: In the Upper Realm, on a terrace of cloud above the western palace, a white tiger the size of a mountain is lying in the sun. As you pass it opens one eye. "You smelled of medicine," it says, "and you held on with one hand. I remember every child I carried. You were the one who did not let go of the jar."

choices.text: Lie down against its flank, as you once slept on its back

effects.log: It is still warm, and still smells of pine and frost, though there is no pine up here and no frost. You sleep, an immortal, like a child, and wake at dawn at the gate of your own hall, with nothing broken.

choices.text: Thank it, at last, properly

effects.log: You bow, a full bow to the ground, the one you were too small and too asleep to make at the gate that dawn. It closes its eye, satisfied. "Errand five," it says, as if to itself. "Done well."

events.text: Rain from a clear sky: the sun shining on the paddies, and fine bright rain falling all the same, glittering. "A tiger is getting married," the old people say, and laugh, and do not go in. Through the shining mist on the far ridge, for one moment, you could swear you see a line of striped shapes walking in procession, the way a wedding walks.

choices.text: Stand in it and wish them well

effects.log: You stand in the bright rain with your face up and say it aloud: long life, many cubs. The rain stops as quickly as it started. On the far ridge, the procession, if it was one, has gone over the top.

choices.text: Run for the ridge to see

effects.log: By the time you reach the ridge it is dry and empty. But the grass is pressed flat in a long line, as if many heavy feet had walked it in step, and caught on a thorn there is a red thread of the kind a bride wears.

events.text: On your own wedding day, or on the day you finally decide you will never have one, it rains from a clear sky. Everyone laughs and says a tiger is marrying too. And under the eaves, out of the bright rain, a magpie lands on the rail and drops something at your feet: a single long white hair.

choices.text: Keep it, for luck

effects.log: You keep it all your life in a fold of paper. Whenever it rains from a clear sky, the paper is warm.

choices.text: Give it back to the rain

effects.log: You hold it out into the rain and let go. It does not fall. It floats away west, glittering, like a thread being drawn back into the loom it came from.

events.text: Autumn equinox. At dusk, in the west, the wind turns cold and clean and smells of cut grain and iron, and for a breath the clouds over the mountains have stripes, and then they do not.

choices.text: Weigh the year honestly

effects.log: You sit on the ridge and count the year: what you did right, what you did wrong, what you only meant to do. The wind waits until you have finished. Then it goes.

choices.text: Breathe in the west wind and meditate

effects.log: The west wind at the equinox is thin and bright as a blade. You breathe it until the three stars of the Balance come out, and go about the next day feeling as if something in you had been sharpened.

events.text: Night guard in the throne hall. You pass the dais a hundred times a night, and every time you pass the white tiger pelt spread down its steps your skin creeps, as if somebody were drawing a knife very slowly down your back. Tonight, at the third watch, you stop in front of it. You know the old scar on its shoulder. You know how the snow felt the morning they came up the mountain with four hundred men.

choices.text: Kneel and put your hand on it

effects.log: The fur is cold, and then, under your palm, very slowly, warm. You hear, or remember, the gongs, the beaters, the sums the captain did out loud. You take your hand away. Your palm smells of pine and frost for a week.

choices.text: Turn the pelt so its face is to the wall

effects.log: It is heavier than it should be. When the court comes in the morning nobody can say who turned it, and the king, oddly, forbids anybody to turn it back.

choices.text: Walk on, and keep walking past it every night

effects.log: You do your rounds. You walk past it a hundred times a night for three years. On the last night of your service you stop and say, under your breath, "We are both still here." Nobody hears. You feel better.

events.text: A sect auction in a lantern-lit hall. The last lot is brought out on black lacquer: a stoppered jar of Tiger Bone Elixir, brewed, the auctioneer says, from the bones of the white tiger of the west itself, the one whose pelt lies on the throne dais. Every bone in your body aches at once, as if it were remembering being somewhere else.

choices.text: Bid for it, whatever it costs (300 taels)

effects.log: Three hundred taels, and the room hates you. When you take the jar, your bones stop aching, all at once, the way a dog stops whining when its owner comes home.

choices.text: Stand up and tell them what is in the jar

ok.log: You tell them: a pass, a captain doing sums, a cauldron, forty days. You do not know how you know. The room goes very quiet. Nobody bids. In the end the sect elder brings the jar to you on its tray and leaves without a word.

fail.log: They laugh you out of the hall. The jar goes to a young master of a great family for four hundred taels. You hear the next year that he drank it, and that he now sleeps only by day, and growls.

choices.text: Leave the hall: you cannot breathe here

effects.log: Outside in the cold you breathe until your bones stop hurting. Through the paper doors you hear the gavel. You never ask who bought it.

events.text: The jar of Tiger Bone Elixir sits on a shelf in your room. On autumn nights it knocks, faintly, from the inside, like something turning over in its sleep. It has taken you years to decide what to do with it.

choices.text: Drink it

ok.log: It goes down like snow-melt and then like fire. For a month your bones are somebody else's. When it passes you are stronger than you have ever been, and you can smell a deer a mountain away, and you never again sleep well under a roof.

fail.deathCause: the Tiger Bone Elixir, which remembered
fail.log: The bones remember.

choices.text: Carry it to the western pass and pour it on the cairn

effects.log: Nine days west. On the cairn at the top of the pass you unstop the jar and pour it out over the stones, slowly. It soaks in. The wind drops. On the rock above the road, for a moment, there is a shape, white, sitting up, and then there is only the rock.

choices.text: Bury the jar, sealed, under the oldest pine you can find

effects.log: You dig with your hands until they bleed, and put it in, and fill it. A magpie watches the whole time from a branch, and when you have finished it laughs, once, not unkindly, and flies off west to tell somebody.

events.text: Hunting bandits in the northern hills, you shelter in an old grave mound that robbers broke open long ago. Inside, by torchlight, the chamber is granite slabs, and on each wall a guardian. On the west wall the white tiger has flaked away so badly that almost nothing is left: only its long stretched neck, its wide-open mouth, and a pair of wings still as orange as the day they were painted. It is looking at the coffin platform. You know, with your whole body, what it felt like to be poured into that wall.

choices.text: Put your hand on the west wall

effects.log: The stone is warm under your palm. In the dark you hear, or remember, a dying king's voice asking for a guardian, and a painter grinding white shell and red earth, and thirteen hundred years of a sleeper breathing in the next room. You take your hand away. There is a little orange on your fingers.

choices.text: Seal the robbers' entrance with stones

effects.log: It takes you a day and a night. When the last stone is in place you hear from inside, very faintly, a long breath let out, like a guard who has been standing a long time and has finally been told to sit.

events.text: A party of court scholars has come north to copy the old tomb murals before they fade entirely. Their head scholar, {npc}, is in despair over the west wall. "There is nothing left of the tiger," {npc} says. "A neck, a mouth, two wings. We cannot copy a tiger that is not there."

choices.text: Describe the tiger to {npc}, stripe by stripe

ok.log: You describe it all afternoon, things nobody living could know: the stripes like brushstrokes of ink on white, the claws, the way the wings were added last because the painter wept. {npc} paints from your words with tears running down. The copy hangs in the royal library for six hundred years.

fail.log: You know it, and cannot say it. {npc} paints the neck, the mouth and the wings alone, very carefully, and the copy of the west wall is the strangest painting in the royal library: an open mouth and two wings, flying.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to leave the west wall as it is

effects.log: "Some guardians," you say, "fade because they are still working." {npc} looks at the orange wings for a long while and leaves a space on the scroll where the west should be.

events.text: All your life you have dreamed now and then of a dark room and a long watch. Tonight the dream is different: the sleeper in the next room has sat up. "Thirteen hundred years," says an old king's voice, cracked with dust. "You may fly now. I am not afraid of the dark any more."

choices.text: Say you were glad to stay

effects.log: You wake with your face wet and your heart very light. All that year, wherever you sleep, you sleep the whole night through.

choices.text: Ask the king what the dark was like

effects.log: "Like being inside a tiger's mouth," the king says, "that had decided not to close." A dry laugh. "I recommend it."

events.text: In the old tomb with the flaking west wall, you look round, by the torch, at the east wall opposite. The dragon there has faded almost to nothing too: only its eye is still bright. And the eye is looking across the chamber at the tiger's open mouth, and the tiger's mouth is open toward the eye, and you understand that for thirteen hundred years they have been keeping each other company in the dark, and that you were both of them.

choices.text: Stand in the middle of the chamber, between them

effects.log: Left, the eye. Right, the mouth. You stand where the sleeper's feet would be and feel the two of them meet in you like two rivers. When you leave, you are not sure for a while which side of your body is which.

choices.text: Bow to the east wall, then to the west

effects.log: East, then west, as a guest would. The torch flame leans toward the eye, then toward the mouth, as if in a draught, though the chamber is perfectly still.

events.text: In the little mountain god hall behind a temple, the painting is the same as in every such hall in the country: an old man with a white beard under a pine, and a tiger at his knee. But tonight, by the candles, you see what nobody else seems to see. The old man has your eyes. So does the tiger.

choices.text: Light the candles and bow, as to an old friend

effects.log: You bow. The painting does not move. But the bowl of clean water on the altar, which you did not touch, ripples once, from the middle outward, the way water answers somebody it knows.

choices.text: Laugh out loud

effects.log: The monk sweeping the courtyard looks in, scandalised. You cannot stop. Both faces in the painting, you would swear, look faintly amused with you.

events.text: A child from the village is lost on the mountain in the first snow, and the searchers have turned back at dark. You have never climbed this mountain in your life. You know, all the same, every path on it: where the spring is, which ledge has a cave, where a frightened child would go to get out of the wind.

choices.text: Go up alone, straight to the place

effects.log: Straight up in the dark without a torch, to a ledge under an overhang, and the child is there, asleep in a hollow in the snow that is the exact shape of a curled tiger and still warm. You carry the child down. Nobody asks how you knew. Everybody wonders.

choices.text: Light a candle at the shrine first and ask

effects.log: You light it and ask, and the answer comes before the wax drips: the ledge under the overhang. You go up, and the child is there, and at the edge of the trees something with a white tail is just leaving, its errand done.

events.text: Walking the ridge above your village in old age, you find a walking staff leaning against the oldest pine, smooth as horn from use, warm from somebody's hand. There is nobody on the mountain. There has been nobody on it all day.

choices.text: Take it up and walk on

effects.log: It fits your hand as if it had been waiting for it. You walk with it for the rest of your life. Children say that when you pass, the mountain goes quiet in a respectful way, like a dog when the master comes in.

choices.text: Leave it for its owner

effects.log: You lean it back against the pine and go on. That night you dream of an old man and a tiger walking a ridge together, both tired, both content, and of neither of them needing a staff any more.

events.text: You have always counted days without meaning to. And on the twentieth day of anything, a fast, a journey, a sickness, a long winter indoors, a terrible hunger comes over you: for raw meat, and open sky, and running. It passes on the twenty-first. It has never once failed to pass. This time it is a fever, and it is the twentieth day.

choices.text: Stay in the dark room and endure it

effects.log: You lie with your face to the wall and your hands in fists until the twenty-first morning comes, and with it the hunger goes, as it always does, and you weep without knowing why, the way somebody weeps who has finally kept a very old promise.

choices.text: Get up and walk out into the sun

effects.log: You stagger out into the yard and stand in the sun, shaking. The hunger goes at once. Your fever comes back worse. Something in you says, quite clearly: not again. You do not know what it means.

events.text: On a mountain in the north there is a cave where, the old people say, a bear once stayed a hundred days in the dark on mugwort and garlic and came out a woman, the mother of the first king; and a tiger stayed with her, and left on the twentieth day. Pilgrims leave mugwort at the mouth. You have come a long way without quite deciding to.

choices.text: Go in and sit in the dark for one day

effects.log: One day in the dark, with a sprig of mugwort in your hand. Near the end of it you hear, very close, the breathing of something large, and then another, smaller, steadier. A bear and a tiger. Then you hear the larger one get up and go. You stay. When you come out it is sunset, and you have never been so glad to see the sky.

choices.text: Leave mugwort and garlic at the mouth, and bow

effects.log: You set them down among the others. Somewhere far back in the cave something stirs and settles. On the way down you are not hungry for the whole long walk, which is a strange thing to notice, and you notice it.

events.text: You dream of a cave. It is the hundredth morning. Light is coming in at the mouth, and you are standing up, on two feet, which feels very strange and very right, and walking out into the sun. Behind you in the dark there are the marks of claws on the stone, ninety-nine scratches in a row.

choices.text: Turn round and look back into the cave

effects.log: In the dark, a tiger is lying where you lay, watching you go, with an expression of enormous patience. It is you. It is also, you think, proud of you. You wake with the sun on your face.

choices.text: Keep walking into the sun

effects.log: You walk out and do not look back, and the sun is warm on a face that has never felt sun before. You wake laughing. All that day ordinary things, rice, a cup, a doorway, seem miraculous.

events.text: A small old temple at the edge of a city that the locals call the Temple the Tiger Wished For. A young hwarang built it long ago, the monks say, for a tiger who loved him and gave her life on his blade so that he could rise. The stones round its pagoda are worn hollow by a thousand years of circling feet. You stand at the edge of the path and cannot breathe.
events.arc: The Temple the Tiger Wished For

choices.text: Circle the pagoda

effects.log: Round and round, as the young people did in the old capital at the spring festival. On the third circuit your feet find a rhythm you did not teach them, and somebody, you would swear, is keeping pace with you, a step behind, on the inside.

choices.text: Ask the monks what became of the hwarang

effects.log: "He grew old in office," the eldest monk says, "and every spring night of his life he circled this pagoda alone. At the end he wrote the story down, so that people would know a tiger can be kind." The monk looks at you oddly. "You are crying. Most people only find it romantic."

events.text: {npc}, a descendant of the hwarang who built the Temple the Tiger Wished For, keeps in the family shrine a plain old sword with a nick in the blade. {npc} has heard you circled the pagoda and wept, and has come to ask you a strange thing. "The family story says," {npc} says, "that one day the tiger would come back as a person, and we must give the blade back. I think the story means you."
events.arc: The Temple the Tiger Wished For

choices.text: Take the sword

effects.log: It is light, and old, and the nick in its edge is exactly where you knew it would be. You hold it a moment, and give it back. "Keep it," you say. "It did what I asked." {npc} bows to the ground and does not get up for a long time.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the story is only a story

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, and at your hands, which are shaking, and says politely that of course it is. On your way out the old sword in the shrine rings once, faintly, like a bell somebody brushed in passing.

events.text: Spring festival night. You go back to the Temple the Tiger Wished For and circle the pagoda with the crowd and the lanterns. Near dawn the crowd thins, and you are alone, and then you are not: somebody old, in a hwarang's faded silk, is circling beside you, and smiles, and is not there.
events.arc: The Temple the Tiger Wished For

choices.text: Keep circling until the bell

effects.log: Round and round until the morning bell. You are not alone on any circuit, though you never see anyone again. When you stop, the stones under your feet are warm in two lines, side by side.

choices.text: Stop and say his name

effects.log: You say it, a name you have never read anywhere. The morning bell rings by itself. The monks come running, and find you sitting on the pagoda step, laughing and crying at once, which, the eldest says, is the correct thing to do in that courtyard.

events.text: Woodcutters in these mountains tell of young tigers seen with white bands round their heads, like mourners' hemp. Nobody believes them. Today, coming over a ridge, you see three: young, striped, sitting in a row in the snow, each with a band of white round its brow, looking down toward a grave you cannot see.

choices.text: Sit down where you are and mourn with them

effects.log: You sit in the snow, a long way off, and bow your head. After a while the three of them look round at you, all together, and then go back to their watching, as if you had been expected.

choices.text: Ask aloud whom they are mourning

effects.log: They do not answer, being tigers. But in your head, quite clearly, comes the picture of a little thatched house with a bowl of rice by the gate, and an old woman cuffing somebody round the ear. You laugh, and then you cannot stop crying.

events.text: {npc}'s family has a strange custom at New Year: a bowl of white rice and a cup of water set out by the gate for "Eldest", whom nobody living has met. "An ancestor of ours called a tiger kin to save a life," {npc} says, "and the tiger kept the lie better than we did. We still owe it supper." {npc} looks at you a long time. "You may eat it, if you like. Grandmother said one day somebody would."

choices.text: Eat the rice

effects.log: You eat the whole bowl standing at the gate, while the family watches in silence. It is plain rice. It is the best meal of your life. When you finish, the old grandmother of the house comes out and cuffs you round the ear, gently, and says, "There. Now go home."

choices.text: Ask {npc} to keep setting it out

effects.log: "For whom?" {npc} asks. "For the next one," you say. {npc} nods slowly. The bowl is still set out every New Year, as far as anyone knows, and every New Year it is empty by morning.

events.text: High on the mountain where you saw the young tigers in their mourning bands, there is an old grave mound, and curled round it under the moss, as if asleep, are the white bones of a great tiger. Nobody has moved them. Nobody would.

choices.text: Clean the moss from both, the grave and the bones

effects.log: A whole day on your knees. When you have finished, the grave and the tiger look the way they must have looked on the first night: an old woman asleep, and somebody keeping her company. You do not raise a cairn. They do not need a pot or a spindle. Nobody here is going anywhere.

choices.text: Sit with them until dusk

effects.log: You sit with your back against the mound and the bones beside you. It is the most peaceful afternoon of your life. At dusk three young tigers come out of the trees, each with a white band round its head, look at you, and go away again, satisfied.

events.text: A village in a valley between two ridges. The villagers put rice at the foot of both at the New Year: Grandfather Dragon on the left, Grandmother Tiger on the right. Standing on the bridge in the middle of the village, you find you cannot stop looking at the right-hand ridge, the low white-rocked one that crouches, and your back aches the way a back aches after lying in one position for a very long time.

choices.text: Climb the right ridge and lie down on it

effects.log: You lie along the crest in the sun with your arms out. The rock is warm. Across the valley, on the left ridge, the pines stir all at once in no wind, as if something over there had lifted its head to see who was lying on the other side, and then put it down again, content.

choices.text: Ask the villagers about the bad years

effects.log: "Bad years?" the innkeeper says. "Once a century the two of them quarrel about the rain, and then it rains on both sides at once and everybody gets wet. That is our bad year." He laughs. "We have no word for the other kind."

events.text: Bandits, a hundred of them, are coming up the road toward the village between the two ridges. The village has no walls. The headman is not worried. "Watch," he says, and goes on with his supper.

choices.text: Watch

effects.log: At the valley mouth the bandits stop. On their right the white ridge has stood up. On their left the green one has lifted its head. They stand very still for a long time. Then they go home the long way, and some of them become farmers.

choices.text: Go down to the valley mouth with your sword

effects.log: You stand at the mouth alone, feeling brave, and then feel the white ridge behind your right shoulder rise and the green one behind your left, and feel considerably less necessary. The bandits flee. The headman sends you a bowl of his supper with a note: thank you for trying.

events.text: Every time it rains from a clear sky, all your life, you have stopped whatever you are doing and stood in it, smiling like a fool, and felt, for the length of the shower, that it is somebody's anniversary and that somebody is you. Today it rains so, over the next mountain, and you cannot help it: you start walking toward it.

choices.text: Walk all the way to the next mountain

effects.log: By the time you reach the foot of it the rain has stopped. But up on the ridge, in the last of the glitter, two old striped shapes are sitting side by side, and below them on the slopes are young tigers everywhere, more than you have ever heard of in one place. One of the old ones turns its head toward you. You raise a hand.

choices.text: Stand still in the rain until it stops

effects.log: You stand in it with your face up. A child going past asks you why you are smiling. "A tiger is getting married," you say. "Again." The child goes off to tell everybody that you are mad, which is fair.

events.text: {npc}, the oldest hunter of three counties, says the hunters grumble that the next mountain has more tigers on it than all the rest of the country, and that not one of them has ever taken a person, and that they are therefore impossible to get a bounty for. They want to drive the mountain anyway, for the pelts.

choices.text: Go to the hunters and talk them out of it

ok.log: You tell them about the sunshowers, and the wedding, and the thousand years. They laugh at you. Then {npc} says that a grandfather in the family told the same story, and that the mountain has never once had a man-eater on it. The drive is called off.

fail.log: They go anyway. They come back in a week with nothing: every time they reached the ridge it rained from a clear sky so hard they could not see their own spears. They do not try again.

choices.text: Walk the next mountain yourself, ahead of the drive, warning

effects.log: You walk the ridges for three days calling out like a fool. On the third, it rains from a clear sky, and through the glitter you see them going, a long procession, over the top and down the far side, unhurried, the way a wedding walks.

events.text: On the day you marry, or the day you decide for good that you will not, it rains from a clear sky. On the ridge of the next mountain two striped shapes are sitting side by side, very old, in the glitter, watching your door.

choices.text: Bow to them

effects.log: You bow. The two old ones lower their heads together. Every rain from a clear sky for the rest of your life, someone in the house says, "Happy anniversary," and nobody knows why it is the custom.

choices.text: Wave

effects.log: You feel ridiculous. One of the old shapes, very slightly, flicks its tail. Your guests think you are waving at the weather. In a way you are.

events.text: You have always known when somebody in the land is about to be put to death. A coldness, a weight, three small points of frost under your breastbone, lined up. You have never told anyone. Today the frost is very sharp, and you are in the same town as the execution ground.

choices.text: Go to the execution ground

effects.log: You stand at the back of the crowd. When the blade falls the frost under your breastbone goes out like a pinched candle, and you know, with complete certainty, that the sentence was just, and that knowing it is no comfort at all.

choices.text: Go the other way, as far as you can walk

effects.log: You walk until dark. The frost goes out at noon anyway, wherever you are. That night you look up at the three small stars below the three bright ones in the western sky and say, aloud, "Not this time." It is not much. It is something.

events.text: {npc}, a magistrate, has heard that you can tell a just sentence from an unjust one by the frost in your chest, and has come in secret to ask you to sit behind the screen at a capital case tomorrow.

choices.text: Sit behind the screen

effects.log: The frost does not come. The sentence would have been wrong. You tell {npc} so, and {npc} believes you, and a person goes home who would not have. That night the three small stars are very faint, as if resting.

choices.text: Refuse: no person should be a scale

effects.log: "Then how will I know?" {npc} asks. "The way everyone else does," you say. "By being afraid of being wrong." {npc} goes away, angry, and, you hear, becomes the most careful magistrate in the province.

events.text: You dream of being three small stars, alone, under a belt of three bright ones, with every death sentence in the land falling through you like hail. Just, very often. Merciful, never. And then, in the dream, somebody on the ground below looks up and waves.

choices.text: Wave back

effects.log: You wave, a star waving. You wake warm for the first time in years, and go out, and find a child in the lane who has been sent to bed early for some crime and is sulking, and you sit with the child and say nothing at all about justice.

choices.text: Stay a star, and keep counting

effects.log: You keep counting, in the dream, sentence after sentence. At dawn you wake knowing exactly how many there were that night, and that every one of them was just, and you get up and go and plant a tree, because it seems the only possible answer.

events.text: New Year, and every gate in the lane has its magpie-and-tiger painting: the magpie on the pine, chattering, and the tiger below, cross-eyed and grinning and absurd. This year, for the first time in your life, you cannot look at them. The tiger's grin is your grin. The magpie, in every painting, is sitting on its head.

choices.text: Paste one on your own gate anyway

effects.log: You paste it up, crooked, and stand back. It is very funny. It is also, you find, a little bit forgiving: the tiger in it is a fool, but it is standing in front of the gate, and nothing evil comes through it all year.

choices.text: Paint your own, with a dignified tiger

ok.log: It takes you a week. The tiger in it is grave and wise and level-eyed. The magpie is nowhere to be seen. Within a month, without anybody touching it, a magpie has been drawn on its head in charcoal by a passing child, and you have to admit it improves it.

fail.log: However hard you try, your tiger comes out cross-eyed. You give up and hang it. The neighbours say it is the best in the lane.

events.text: On the pass above the village, bandits have held the road for a generation, and a man-eater holds the mountain behind it, and the old people say there used to be a tiger on that mountain that forgave everybody, which is how this happened. A magpie lands on your shoulder and laughs in your ear.

choices.text: Go up and clear the pass

ok.log: You clear it. Not cruelly; not gently either. Every bandit who is willing goes home. The three who are not, do not. On the way down the magpie rides on your head, and for once it does not laugh.

fail.log: There are too many of them. But they know now that somebody is coming, and two of them go home of their own accord. (-18 health)

choices.text: Forgive them, and go home

effects.log: You go home. The magpie follows you all the way, laughing so hard it falls off a branch. You lie awake that night wondering whether mercy and laziness have ever been told apart by anybody.

events.text: An old folk painter at the New Year market looks up from a stack of magpie-and-tiger paintings, sees you, and drops the brush. "Sit," the painter says. "I have drawn your face ten thousand times and never seen it."

choices.text: Sit for the painting

effects.log: An hour. When the painter turns it round, the tiger in it is still cross-eyed, still grinning, but it is standing up, and the magpie on its head is looking at it with something like respect. "That one is not for sale," the painter says, and gives it to you.

choices.text: Laugh and buy ten of the usual ones

effects.log: Three taels for ten fools. You give them to every house on your lane that does not have one. That year, every gate in the lane has a tiger on it that is laughing at itself, which, the old people say, is the strongest kind.

events.text: There is a pass in the west that nobody has crossed after dark for three hundred years. The road is grass. At dusk, the villagers at its foot say, voices come down it, calling names in the voices of mothers. You have come here without meaning to. As the light goes, the voices begin, and every one of them is calling, not a traveller's name, but yours.

choices.text: Walk up the pass toward them

ok.log: Nine of them, standing along the road in their rags, and as you come up they fall silent one by one and look at you, the way servants look at a master who has come back after a long time away. "Let us go," the first one says. "You could. You are the only one who could." You are shaking. You say yes.

fail.log: Halfway up the voices change, and every one of them is somebody you have loved in this life, and your legs give. You crawl back down. You will have to come back. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stay at the foot of the pass and answer them, one by one

effects.log: All night, sitting on a stone at the foot of the road, you answer each voice in turn: not your own name, but theirs, the names they had before. You do not know how you know them. By dawn there are only four voices left calling.

events.text: You have come back to the ghost pass with nine steamer pots, nine iron spindles, a shaman, and a cart of stones. The shaman thinks you mean to fix them under the pots for ever. You are not sure yet what you mean.

choices.text: Build nine cairns, and leave the spindles out

effects.log: Nine cairns, nine pots turned over, and then, at the end, nine spindles laid in a row on the grass and not driven home. "That is not the rite," the shaman says. "No," you say. "It is the apology." At dawn there are no voices on the pass. That spring the first traveller in three hundred years walks over it alone at dusk, singing.

choices.text: Do it the old way: pot and spindle, all nine

effects.log: Nine pots, nine spindles. The pass goes silent. Inside each pot something goes round and round, for ever, like thread. The villagers are overjoyed and cross the pass freely. You never do. You cannot bear the sound the pots make, which nobody else can hear.

events.text: Crossing any pass at dusk, all your life, you have heard footsteps a little way behind you, keeping pace, that stop when you stop. Tonight, at the top of a pass in a strange province, they come up level with you for the first time. A young porter in a torn jacket walks beside you, and bows, and walks on ahead, and is gone.

choices.text: Call after the porter

effects.log: You call. The porter turns, at the bottom of the far slope, and waves, the way a person waves who has finally been let go home. After that night you never hear footsteps behind you again, and you miss them, a little.

choices.text: Stand still until the footsteps have gone

effects.log: You stand until the last sound is gone down the far side of the pass. It is the quietest night of your life. You walk on alone, which, after so many years, feels like a great gift and a small grief.

events.text: You have always been afraid of ropes: not of hanging, not of falling, but of asking for a rope and being given one. And of red sorghum. Today, crossing a field of it in autumn, red from root to tassel, you find yourself on your knees in the middle of it with no memory of kneeling.

choices.text: Stay on your knees and say sorry to the field

effects.log: You do not know what for. The field seems to. The wind goes over the red stalks in one long sigh, and when you stand up the stalks nearest you are a little paler than the rest, as if something had been taken off them.

choices.text: Get up and walk out, fast

effects.log: You get out of the field and do not look back. That night you dream of climbing, and of the sound a rope makes just before it gives, and wake with your hands clenched on nothing.

events.text: A brother and a sister from your village, orphaned this winter, have been put out of their house by an uncle who wears their dead mother's coat to the market and lies about the will. Everybody knows. Nobody does anything. You feel, watching the uncle in that coat, a sickness you cannot explain, as if you were watching yourself.

choices.text: Take the uncle to the magistrate

ok.log: It takes a month and every favour you have. The house goes back to the children. The uncle has to give back the coat in front of the whole market. You find, when it is done, that something very old in you has finally stopped falling.

fail.log: The magistrate sides with the uncle. So you take the children into your own house. It is not justice. It is a roof.

choices.text: Take the children in and say nothing to anyone

effects.log: Two more bowls at your table. The uncle keeps the house and the coat. That winter you hear he climbed onto his own roof to mend it and the old rope he tied himself to snapped. He lived. He never wore the coat again.

events.text: You dream of a tree at night, and two children high in it, and a rope coming down to them from heaven, strong and shining. Below, at the foot of the tree, something in borrowed clothes is looking up and opening its mouth to ask for a rope of its own. You know whose mouth that is.

choices.text: Do not ask

effects.log: In the dream you close the mouth and do not ask. You take off the borrowed clothes and fold them and leave them at the foot of the tree. The children climb into the sky and become the sun and the moon. You wake on the ground of yourself, safe, never having fallen.

choices.text: Ask for a ladder instead, and climb it slowly

effects.log: A ladder comes down, plain wood, very long. You climb it a rung a year. In the dream it takes a thousand years. You wake rested, and that day you start something slow that you will not live to finish, and are glad.

events.text: Every year at the first snow you wake before dawn knowing it has come, before you see it, the way a cub knows its mother's tongue in the dark. This year, walking in the hills on the morning of the first snow, you find a den in the rocks with a single striped cub in it, blind, asleep, and the snow just beginning to drift in at the mouth.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Kneel at the mouth of the den and shelter it from the snow

effects.log: You kneel with your back to the wind until your shoulders are white. The cub sleeps on. Near noon a huge shape comes down the slope, sees you, and stops. You get up and walk away backwards, slowly. Behind you, the mother goes in, and the cub makes a sound you remember from somewhere very far away.

choices.text: Leave it, and do not tell anyone

effects.log: You go, and you tell nobody. All winter you think of it. It is, you think, beginning again, remembering everything. You hope it does better. You suspect it will.

events.text: Years later, at the first snow, a young tiger with a white tip to its tail sits down on a rock above the road you are walking, and looks at you, and you know it: the cub from the den. It looks at you as if it knew you too, from further back than that.
events.arc: The Den in the First Snow

choices.text: Stand still and keep your head

effects.log: You stand. It watches you stand. Then it does the thing you half expected: it stretches like a cat in front of a fire and walks off along the ridge, and at the top it looks back once, and you could swear it laughs.

choices.text: Throw it a rice cake

effects.log: It eats the rice cake with enormous seriousness and looks at you a long time. "Again?" the look says. "Again," you say aloud. It goes up the slope and walks along the ridge above you, keeping pace, all the way to the village lights.

events.text: A young tomb painter, painting the guardian of the west in a lord's burial chamber, has never seen a tiger and paints it with eyes closed, "from memory, the way everyone does". You hold the lamp. When the head is done you recognise it. It is the look you give yourself in a basin of water in the morning, when you are deciding something.

choices.text: Tell the painter it is a good likeness

effects.log: The painter laughs, thinking you are joking. You are not. All your life after that, whenever you pass the west wall of any old shrine, the painted tiger seems to give you a small, level look of recognition.

choices.text: Ask the painter who taught that face

effects.log: "Nobody," the painter says. "Every painter just knows it, since the Guardian took the west wall of the sky. It is in the hand." The painter shrugs. "The hard part is the eyes. They have to be fair. Nobody can teach fair."

events.text: On a clear autumn night you look up at the seven stars of the western sky, Legs to the Three Stars, and for the first time in this life they are not stars: they are a body, long and crouched, and the three straight stars of the Balance are its heart, and they are perfectly level, and it is looking down at you and at everyone else.

choices.text: Look back for as long as it looks down

effects.log: Until dawn. It does not blink. You do, eventually. When the sun comes up you find you are no longer afraid of being judged, by anyone, for anything you have done in this life.

choices.text: Weigh your own year, honestly, under it

effects.log: You sit on the cold ground and weigh the year, the way it weighs every year. The beam in your chest comes out level, just. You go to bed grinning like a child who has passed an examination.

events.text: A village shaman is performing the rite of the five directions at harvest: five colours of cloth, five generals called, and for the west, the White Emperor, who is autumn. The shaman spins west with a white fan and stops dead, facing you. The bells go silent. "Oh," the shaman says, in an entirely different voice. "It is you. It is very strange to be called by yourself."

choices.text: Answer the voice

effects.log: "Hello," you say, feeling foolish. The voice laughs, and every leaf on every tree in the village falls at once, red and gold, and the harvest that year is weighed and found exactly enough, which in that village has never happened before.

choices.text: Bow, and let the rite go on

effects.log: You bow to the shaman and to whatever is in the shaman. The voice says, "Fair. Good," and goes, and the rite carries on, north to the Black Tortoise, east to the Azure Dragon. But the west wind that night is clean and cold and smells of cut grain.

events.text: An early frost has threatened the harvest in three provinces, and the grain is standing green in the fields with winter coming. You walk out into the fields at dusk and, without knowing why, breathe out toward the west as hard as you can.

choices.text: Breathe again, with all your qi

ok.log: The west wind comes back to you like an echo, dry and warm and golden, and goes over the fields, and the green grain is gold by morning, ripe a fortnight early, in front of the frost. The farmers tell it for generations and get the name wrong. You do not correct them.

fail.log: You breathe until you fall over. Nothing. Then, three days later, a long dry wind from the west, enough to bring in most of it. You are never sure. (-10 health)

choices.text: Help the farmers cut it green and dry it in the barns

effects.log: Green grain dried on every rack and rafter in three villages. It is not a good harvest. It is not a hungry winter. In the spring every rack you hung grain on puts out, absurdly, a single red leaf.

events.text: In the Upper Realm there is a palace in the west where it is always the evening of the harvest. The gatekeeper does not ask your name. "The Emperor is out," {npc} says, "being autumn somewhere. But the Emperor said that if you ever came you were to be let in, and given new rice, and that you would know the way."

choices.text: Go in and sit on the empty throne for one breath

effects.log: One breath. In it you feel every harvest there has ever been, every account settled, every field weighed, all at once, level. You get up before the second breath, which, the gatekeeper tells you afterwards, is the right number.

choices.text: Eat the new rice and leave a note

effects.log: The rice tastes of the first harvest after a famine. Your note says only: a rock above a pass, the first snow. {npc} folds it carefully. "The Emperor will laugh," {npc} says. "The Emperor does not laugh enough."
